sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-PDCORP-3.1 used to recalibrate the Corporate Rating Model PD-CORP-MM v3.1 (inventory identifier MDL-06), which assigns obligor ratings and one-year PDs to the Bank's mid-market corporate clients: non-financial corporates with consolidated annual revenue from EUR 25 million up to EUR 500 million, booked in the Netherlands and in the German and Belgian branches. The same RDS was used for risk differentiation (development of the financial and qualitative modules for v3.0 in 2022, re-tested in 2025) and for risk quantification (long-run average calibration of v3.1); where the two uses differ in sample, this is stated per section. The rating system is used for own funds requirements under the IRB approach for the corporate exposure class, for which the Bank has held permission since 2008; the experience test is met. The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A and is the first issue of the RDS documentation of this model in that template; it is stored in DocHub (folder MDL-06/RDS) with version control and a document history in chapter 9. Cover block: title RDS documentation Corporate Mid-Market PD; model PD-CORP-MM v3.1 (MDL-06); document version 0.9; status draft for review; author A. Hoekstra; reviewer L. Meijer; approver P. van Dijk (Model Owner); not yet approved.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains quarterly obligor observations with reference dates from 31 March 2008 to 31 December 2024 (68 reference dates), each followed by a one-year outcome window, so that default outcomes are observed up to 31 December 2025. It contains 412,600 obligor-quarter observations of 11,480 unique obligors and 1,386 default events (after merging multiple defaults), of which 1,302 obligors defaulted once and 42 twice with more than twelve months between the events. With seventeen years of data, the observation period exceeds the minimum of five years for non-retail PD estimation of CRR Article 180(1)(h) and CRM-STD-100 §6.2, and the longer period is used because the data are available and relevant. The development sample of the risk differentiation modules (v3.0, reference dates 2008–2020) contains 961 defaults and 311,200 obligor-quarters; the default proportion of 0.31% per quarterly observation corresponds to a one-year default rate of 1.55% and is close to the 1.48% one-year default rate of the application portfolio in 2025.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in 2008 because financial statements have been stored in the spreading tool FinSpread with obligor identifiers since January 2007, which allows one year of history before the first reference date; earlier ratings were produced by the previous rating system and cannot be linked reliably to financial data. The window contains the financial crisis (2008–2009), the Dutch recession of 2012–2013, the COVID-19 contraction of 2020 and the energy price shock of 2022, and therefore covers a representative mix of good and bad years including downturn periods, as shown in section 2.3. Two changes in the rating process fall in the window: the introduction of the v2 rating system in 2014 and of v3.0 in December 2024; ratings produced under earlier systems are stored with the system version, and the risk drivers were recomputed from the stored financial statements with the current definitions for the whole window. Lending standards changed in 2014, when the Bank reduced its appetite for commercial real estate developers and construction companies in the mid-market segment; the share of these sectors fell from 21% of obligors in 2008–2013 to 9% in 2020–2024, which is analysed in section 5.1.2.

sections.heading: Long-run average window and good and bad years
sections.text: Yearly one-year default rates (1 January cohorts) range from 0.7% (2021) to 3.4% (2009): 1.9% (2008), 3.4%, 2.1%, 1.8%, 2.3%, 2.6%, 1.7%, 1.3%, 1.1%, 0.9%, 0.8%, 0.9%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 0.8%, 1.1% and 1.3% (2024). Yearly default rates correlate significantly with Dutch real GDP growth (correlation −0.71, p < 0.01) and with the change in the unemployment rate (0.64), which supports the use of these indicators to classify years. A year is classified as bad if real GDP growth is below 0%; this documented criterion classifies 2009, 2012, 2013 and 2020 as bad years, which all show above-average default rates except 2020, in which government support measures suppressed defaults. The share of bad years in the window is 4 of 17 (23.5%), which is not smaller than the reference share over the last 20 years of the GDP series (2006–2025: 4 of 20, 20%). The maximum observed one-year default rate (2009, 3.4%) is included in the window. The window includes observations beyond the most recent five years, which is needed to reflect the likely range of variability of default rates; the treatment of the COVID-19 years in the LRA is described in MDD section 5.1.

sections.text: Not applicable in the sense of the template condition: the target is the regulatory default event under CR-STD-110 within a twelve-month horizon after the reference date, so no separate target definition is required. For the qualitative module the development additionally used agency rating-implied default probabilities of externally rated obligors as a shadow-rating target; that sample and its target are described in MDD section 4.3 and are not part of the calibration. The default flag is taken at obligor level; for each obligor-quarter observation the target equals one if the obligor defaulted at any time within the following twelve months.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable: the RDS default flag for periods from 1 January 2016 is the production flag, which implements CR-STD-110 without deviation, and the reconstruction for 2008–2015 described in section 3.3.4 aims at the same definition. The definition is identical for IRB, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management in all Group entities including the German and Belgian branches, and the prudential and accounting default indicators are labelled distinctly in the RDS. A single definition of default applies to the whole range of application and is applied consistently to the same historical observations used in the PD model and in the corporate LGD model (MDL-07), so the rating system does not encompass different definitions. The definition and its scope were approved by the Group Risk Committee after endorsement by the Model Risk Committee, and the flag is used in own funds calculations, credit monitoring and internal reporting to management.

sections.heading: Default definition – days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when it is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay, and any principal, interest or fee not paid when due is recognised as past due. For the corporate exposures in scope the materiality threshold is the one set by the ECB for all significant institutions under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171: EUR 500 absolute and 1% relative. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposures excluding equity exposures. The dpd counter starts on the first day both components are exceeded, restarts when either is no longer exceeded, and the obligor defaults when both components have been exceeded for 90 consecutive days, i.e. on the 91st day; no months-in-arrears proxies are used. Exposures of the German and Belgian branches are denominated in euro, and 1.2% of exposures in USD and GBP are converted at the daily ECB reference rate; the EUR threshold is applied without currency adjustment. Where a payment schedule is modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule; instalments suspended under contractual rights or by law, including the 2020 COVID-19 deferrals granted to 412 obligors, were not counted as past due and were assessed for unlikeliness to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed obligations only where the dispute is before a court or other formal binding procedure (27 cases in the RDS).

sections.heading: Default definition – level of application, contagion and date of default
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level, and all credit obligations of a defaulted obligor are flagged as defaulted in all systems and in all Group entities without additional expert judgement once the past due criterion is met. For groups of connected clients the credit officer assesses case by case, within 30 days, whether the default of one group entity is contagious to the other entities, using the criteria in CR-STD-110 §4.3 (economic dependence, cross-default clauses, shared cash pool); 61 contagion defaults are recorded in the RDS. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; dpd counters are computed daily, so the date of default equals the date the past due criterion was fulfilled, and it is recorded for every default event. The branches exchange client data with the head office without legal impediments, so default identification is consistent across entities; the triggers are implemented identically in all branches.

sections.heading: Default definition – probation periods and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by the Financial Restructuring and Recovery department (FR&R) that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent; after a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least twelve months and requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no past due amounts and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event. A default within twelve months of return to non-default status is merged with the previous event, keeping the first default date; 55 events were merged, and each defaulted obligor is counted only once in the numerator and denominator of a one-year default rate even if it defaulted more than once in that year. Re-default rates are analysed annually: of the 188 obligors cured in 2021–2024, 11.2% re-defaulted within twelve months, concentrated in cures after forbearance (19.0%); FR&R concluded in October 2025 that the probation rules remain adequate but that forborne cures are monitored quarterly.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – automatic triggers
sections.text: Automatic UTP triggers are: non-accrued status; specific credit risk adjustment or IFRS 9 Stage 3; sale of credit obligations with a credit-related economic loss above 5%; distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; filing for bankruptcy or suspension of payments by the obligor or by the Bank; and forced sale of collateral. Only specific credit risk adjustments reflecting a significant perceived decline in credit quality count as UTP; collective Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances do not. The diminished financial obligation is (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 at the original effective interest rate; forborne exposures below 1% are assessed for other UTP indications (large balloon, back-loaded schedule, significant grace period, repeated forbearance), and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which is verified monthly against the forbearance register. For each sale of corporate loans the reasons and the loss L = (E − P)/E are documented by FR&R; the one portfolio sale in the window (2016, 23 obligors, loss 31%) was recorded as default at the moment of sale for the obligors not yet in default.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – indicators assessed case by case
sections.text: Case-by-case UTP indicators for corporates include breach of financial covenants, significant decline in revenue or cash flow, loss of a major customer, request for emergency funding, fraud, multiple forbearance, adverse audit opinion and default of a group entity; the credit officer completes the assessment within 30 days and records the outcome with its rationale in the credit file. External information is used, including the Dutch and German credit registers, Chamber of Commerce filings, the Graydon and Creditreform credit alerts, sector outlooks and press reports. For each indicator the identification method, sources, monitoring frequency and responsibilities are laid down in the corporate UTP procedure WCR-P-031, and the watchlist and forborne exposure lists are reviewed monthly. Because UTP decisions are expert-based, FR&R applies a labelling guideline with worked examples and performs an annual consistency review of UTP decisions across credit teams; the 2025 review found no systematic differences between teams (UTP share 41–46% of defaults per team). Technical past due situations are recognised only in the cases listed in EBA/GL/2016/07, corrected within 30 days, and the 41 technical past due events are removed from the RDS default events.

sections.heading: Data sources
sections.text: The RDS combines the corporate rating tool CorpRate (ratings, qualitative answers, overrides, rating dates and raters since 2014) and its predecessor RateWise (2007–2014), the spreading tool FinSpread (financial statements), the loan administration system LoanIQ (exposures, limits, arrears), the default register DefaultHub and the watchlist and forbearance registers. Each source belongs to a data domain with exactly one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue (Wholesale Lending, Credit Risk Data, Wholesale Credit Operations), and the authoritative source of each data type is defined: CorpRate for ratings, FinSpread for financial statements, LoanIQ for exposures and DefaultHub for defaults. Common obligors across sources are identified with the Group counterparty identifier, so each obligor is counted only once in the one-year default rates even where it holds exposures in several legal entities. External ratings of S&P, Moody's and Fitch for 612 obligors are obtained through the Bank's market data licence; they are used only in the shadow-rating development of the qualitative module and as benchmark, not in the calibration. No pooled data are used, and no external default data enter the calibration.

sections.heading: Lineage and critical data elements
sections.text: Lineage from the source systems to the RDS is documented for every variable in RDS Annex A, including source table and field, intermediate stores, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build code, and extraction frequency and timing; discarded variables used to construct retained variables (for example the raw balance sheet items behind the seven ratios) are included. For the external ratings the lineage starts at receipt in the market data platform and records the provider, the data product and the delivery date. All model input variables and the elements of the target (default flag, default date, obligor scope flags) are critical data elements with business and technical definitions and DQ rules per applicable dimension. The only manual steps are the version-controlled mapping of RateWise industry codes to NACE Rev. 2 and the list of wrongly scoped obligors identified by Wholesale Credit Operations; both are identified in the lineage with their four-eyes control and documented as expert judgement. The lineage was updated in October 2025 for the migration of LoanIQ to the cloud platform before those data were used, and the Data Owners confirmed that changes to definitions or transformations will be approved by them and communicated in advance.

sections.heading: Rating histories and timing of risk drivers
sections.text: For every obligor the RDS stores the complete rating history: rating dates, model version, score, grade before and after override, override reason, qualitative answers, the financial statement used and the rater and approver, as well as the identity and date and circumstances of each default and the PD and realised default rate per grade. Risk drivers are taken as they were available at each reference date: the financial ratios from the latest financial statement available at that date (not the statement of the reference year), and the qualitative answers from the latest approved rating; for defaulted obligors the values are therefore available throughout the year before default. The median age of the financial statement at the reference date is 9 months; 6.8% of obligor-quarters use a statement older than 18 months and 2.9% one older than 24 months, which is treated in the model as described in MDD section 4.5. Loan-by-loan data, including the ratings, overrides and credit-granting criteria applied at origination, are captured in CorpRate and LoanIQ so that deviations, exceptions and overrides can be tracked.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Each exclusion is documented with its reason, number of observations, share and defaults, and was approved by the Model Owner on 5 February 2026 (ticket WCRM-3318): X1 – obligors wrongly assigned to the model scope at the reference date (revenue outside EUR 25–500 million after correction, financial institutions, specialised lending), 9,850 obligor-quarters (2.4%) and 18 defaults, removed from numerator and denominator; X2 – technical past due default events, 41 events, removed from the numerator only because they were wrongly classified as defaults. Obligors without any on- or off-balance-sheet credit obligation at the start of the period are not part of the default rate denominator by definition (6,120 obligor-quarters, 1.5%). Obligors without a valid rating at the start of a period (3,480 obligor-quarters, 0.8%, default rate 3.9%) are not excluded: they are included in the portfolio-level default rates and analysed separately. Obligors that migrate to another model or approach, repay or whose loans are sold or written off during the year remain in the one-year default rate of their cohort; the resulting bias was analysed and is negligible (effect on the LRA below 0.01 percentage points). No exclusion exceeds 5% of observations or exposure in any segment, and the conclusions of the impact analysis are given in section 5.3.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in RDS Annex C: financial ratios missing for a structural reason (for example interest coverage for obligors without interest-bearing debt, 3.1%) receive the value of the best bucket, and ratios missing because of a data deficiency (1.8%) receive the bucket with the highest observed default rate, in development and production alike. The share of imputed values per variable is reported in Annex C (maximum 4.4% for revenue growth), and re-estimating the financial module without the imputed observations changes no coefficient by more than 6%. Outliers of financial ratios are identified with documented percentile criteria and winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles of the development sample; the same caps are stored in the CorpRate parameter table and applied in production, and the effect of capping on the AUC is below 0.002. The default flag and default date are never imputed; 12 events with unclear default dates were resolved with FR&R from the credit files.

sections.heading: Construction of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated for each of the 68 quarterly reference dates using overlapping one-year windows: the denominator comprises obligors in scope with a credit obligation and not in default at the reference date, the numerator those among them with at least one default in the following twelve months. Grades at the start of each window are the final grades after override, without substitution effects of guarantees or ex post conservative adjustments. The same exclusion and adjustment rules are applied to the calibration data, the monitoring data and the data used in the annual review of estimates. The calibration sample per reference date and grade is stored in the frozen RDS (table calib_sample) and described in MDD section 5.2.

sections.heading: Representativeness – scope and risk drivers
sections.text: Representativeness is assessed under the Bank's representativeness policy (CRM-STD-100 §6.5 and MV-HB-003 §6), which specifies the PSI per risk driver and score, with green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25 and red above 0.25, and a two-sample test of default rates, separately for the development data of the modules and for the calibration data. The scope of the RDS equals the current range of application; against the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 (6,880 obligors), the PSI is 0.05 for the score, below 0.10 for six of the seven financial ratios and all qualitative questions, and 0.13 for revenue growth, which is explained by the inflation-driven nominal revenue growth of 2022–2024 and does not affect the ranking. Missing-value shares are 1.9% in the RDS and 1.4% in the application portfolio.

sections.heading: Representativeness – default rate levels, lending standards and economic conditions
sections.text: Representativeness of default rate levels: the 2023–2024 one-year default rates (1.1% and 1.3%) do not differ significantly from the RDS rates for the same grades (two-sample test of proportions per grade, no significant difference at 5% for 19 of 20 grades), and the current portfolio's average grade is similar to that of the RDS. The change of lending standards in 2014 was analysed by comparing RDS data before and after: default rates of construction and real estate development obligors were 2.1 times those of other sectors in 2008–2013 and 1.5 times afterwards; because the model's sector outlook question and the financial ratios capture most of this difference, no separate adjustment was made, and the remaining uncertainty is covered by MoC category B (B-01). Recovery policies and the legal environment (Dutch insolvency law, including the WHOA restructuring procedure introduced in 2021) were assessed; WHOA restructurings are treated as distressed restructurings and are reflected in the 2021–2024 data. Economic conditions in the RDS include severe recession years and are relevant to current and foreseeable conditions.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The impact of each exclusion on the long-run average default rate and on the risk driver distributions was quantified: X1 changes the LRA by +0.02 percentage points (the excluded obligors have a lower default rate), X2 by −0.05 percentage points, and the combined effect of all exclusions is −0.03 percentage points (−2% relative). The PSI of the score between the RDS before and after exclusions is below 0.01, and the grade distribution is unchanged, so the exclusions do not affect representativeness.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-PDCORP-3.1 used to recalibrate the Corporate Rating Model PD-CORP-MM v3.1 (inventory identifier MDL-06), which assigns obligor ratings and one-year PDs to the Bank's mid-market corporate clients: non-financial corporates with consolidated annual revenue from EUR 25 million up to EUR 500 million, booked in the Netherlands and in the German and Belgian branches. The same RDS was used for risk differentiation (development of the financial and qualitative modules for v3.0 in 2022, re-tested in 2025) and for risk quantification (long-run average calibration of v3.1); where the two uses differ in sample, this is stated per section. The rating system is used for own funds requirements under the IRB approach for the corporate exposure class, for which the Bank has held permission since 2008; the experience test is met. The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A and is the first issue of the RDS documentation of this model in that template; it is stored in DocHub (folder MDL-06/RDS) with version control and a document history in chapter 9. sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains quarterly obligor observations with reference dates from 31 March 2008 to 31 December 2024 (68 reference dates), each followed by a one-year outcome window, so that default outcomes are observed up to 31 December 2025. It contains 412,600 obligor-quarter observations of 11,480 unique obligors and 1,386 default events (after merging multiple defaults), of which 1,302 obligors defaulted once and 42 twice with more than twelve months between the events. With seventeen years of data, the observation period exceeds the minimum of five years for non-retail PD estimation of CRR Article 180(1)(h) and CRM-STD-100 §6.2, and the longer period is used because the data are available and relevant. The development sample of the risk differentiation modules (v3.0, reference dates 2008–2020) contains 961 defaults and 311,200 obligor-quarters; the default proportion of 0.31% per quarterly observation corresponds to a one-year default rate of 1.55% and is close to the 1.48% one-year default rate of the application portfolio in 2025.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in 2008 because financial statements have been stored in the spreading tool FinSpread with obligor identifiers since January 2007, which allows one year of history before the first reference date; earlier ratings were produced by the previous rating system and cannot be linked reliably to financial data. The window contains the financial crisis (2008–2009), the Dutch recession of 2012–2013, the COVID-19 contraction of 2020 and the energy price shock of 2022, and therefore covers a representative mix of good and bad years including downturn periods, as shown in section 2.3. Two changes in the rating process fall in the window: the introduction of the v2 rating system in 2014 and of v3.0 in December 2024; ratings produced under earlier systems are stored with the system version, and the risk drivers were recomputed from the stored financial statements with the current definitions for the whole window. Lending standards changed in 2014, when the Bank reduced its appetite for commercial real estate developers and construction companies in the mid-market segment; the share of these sectors fell from 21% of obligors in 2008–2013 to 9% in 2020–2024, which is analysed in section 5.1.2.

sections.heading: Long-run average window and good and bad years
sections.text: Yearly one-year default rates (1 January cohorts) range from 0.7% (2021) to 3.4% (2009): 1.9% (2008), 3.4%, 2.1%, 1.8%, 2.3%, 2.6%, 1.7%, 1.3%, 1.1%, 0.9%, 0.8%, 0.9%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 0.8%, 1.1% and 1.3% (2024). Yearly default rates correlate significantly with Dutch real GDP growth (correlation −0.71, p < 0.01) and with the change in the unemployment rate (0.64), which supports the use of these indicators to classify years. A year is classified as bad if real GDP growth is below 0%; this documented criterion classifies 2009, 2012, 2013 and 2020 as bad years, which all show above-average default rates except 2020, in which government support measures suppressed defaults. The share of bad years in the window is 4 of 17 (23.5%), which is not smaller than the reference share over the last 20 years of the GDP series (2006–2025: 4 of 20, 20%). The maximum observed one-year default rate (2009, 3.4%) is included in the window. The window includes observations beyond the most recent five years, which is needed to reflect the likely range of variability of default rates; the treatment of the COVID-19 years in the LRA is described in MDD section 5.1.

sections.heading: Default definition – days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when it is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay, and any principal, interest or fee not paid when due is recognised as past due. For the corporate exposures in scope the materiality threshold is the one set by the ECB for all significant institutions under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171: EUR 500 absolute and 1% relative. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposures excluding equity exposures. The dpd counter starts on the first day both components are exceeded, restarts when either is no longer exceeded, and the obligor defaults when both components have been exceeded for 90 consecutive days, i.e. on the 91st day; no months-in-arrears proxies are used. Exposures of the German and Belgian branches are denominated in euro, and 1.2% of exposures in USD and GBP are converted at the daily ECB reference rate; the EUR threshold is applied without currency adjustment. Where a payment schedule is modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule; instalments suspended under contractual rights or by law, including the 2020 COVID-19 deferrals granted to 412 obligors, were not counted as past due and were assessed for unlikeliness to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed obligations only where the dispute is before a court or other formal binding procedure (27 cases in the RDS).

sections.heading: Default definition – level of application, contagion and date of default
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level, and all credit obligations of a defaulted obligor are flagged as defaulted in all systems and in all Group entities without additional expert judgement once the past due criterion is met. For groups of connected clients the credit officer assesses case by case, within 30 days, whether the default of one group entity is contagious to the other entities, using the criteria in CR-STD-110 §4.3 (economic dependence, cross-default clauses, shared cash pool); 61 contagion defaults are recorded in the RDS. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; dpd counters are computed daily, so the date of default equals the date the past due criterion was fulfilled, and it is recorded for every default event. The branches exchange client data with the head office without legal impediments, so default identification is consistent across entities; the triggers are implemented identically in all branches.

sections.heading: Default definition – probation periods and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by the Financial Restructuring and Recovery department (FR&R) that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent; after a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least twelve months and requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no past due amounts and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event. A default within twelve months of return to non-default status is merged with the previous event, keeping the first default date; 55 events were merged, and each defaulted obligor is counted only once in the numerator and denominator of a one-year default rate even if it defaulted more than once in that year. Re-default rates are analysed annually: of the 188 obligors cured in 2021–2024, 11.2% re-defaulted within twelve months, concentrated in cures after forbearance (19.0%); FR&R concluded in October 2025 that the probation rules remain adequate but that forborne cures are monitored quarterly. For 2008–2015 probation periods could not be reconstructed because cure dates were not recorded; cures in that period are approximated by three consecutive months without arrears or forbearance, as stated in section 3.3.4.

sections.heading: Historical approximation of the default flag
sections.text: Three default-definition periods are distinguished (field dod_regime): P1 from 2008 to 2015, in which default is reconstructed from arrears, forbearance, provisioning and bankruptcy data; P2 from January 2016 to November 2020, with the production flag based on an internal threshold of EUR 250 and no relative component; and P3 from December 2020 with the current definition and the regulatory threshold. For P1 the past due criterion was reconstructed from daily arrears in the loan administration system with the EUR 500 / 1% threshold, and UTP from specific provisions, bankruptcy (faillissement and surseance van betaling) registrations and forbearance flags; for P2 the flag was re-derived from daily arrears with the regulatory threshold, which removed 1.1% of P2 default events and added none. The effect of the approximation on default rates was quantified by applying the P1 reconstruction rules to P3 data: the reconstructed flag reproduces 96.1% of P3 defaults, misses 3.9% (mainly UTP defaults without provision) and adds 1.4% false defaults, so P1 default rates are estimated to be understated by about 2.5% relative. The production flag and the RDS flag agree for 99.5% of P3 default events on obligor and date; the remaining 7 cases are retroactive corrections in the default register. The deficiency is logged as DD-PD-01 and linked to MoC category A (A-01).

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – automatic triggers
sections.text: Automatic UTP triggers are: non-accrued status; specific credit risk adjustment or IFRS 9 Stage 3; sale of credit obligations with a credit-related economic loss above 5%; distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; filing for bankruptcy or suspension of payments by the obligor or by the Bank; and forced sale of collateral. Only specific credit risk adjustments reflecting a significant perceived decline in credit quality count as UTP; collective Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances do not. The diminished financial obligation is (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 at the original effective interest rate; forborne exposures below 1% are assessed for other UTP indications (large balloon, back-loaded schedule, significant grace period, repeated forbearance), and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which is verified monthly against the forbearance register. For each sale of corporate loans the reasons and the loss L = (E − P)/E are documented by FR&R; the one portfolio sale in the window (2016, 23 obligors, loss 31%) was recorded as default at the moment of sale for the obligors not yet in default.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – indicators assessed case by case
sections.text: Case-by-case UTP indicators for corporates include breach of financial covenants, significant decline in revenue or cash flow, loss of a major customer, request for emergency funding, fraud, multiple forbearance, adverse audit opinion and default of a group entity; the credit officer completes the assessment within 30 days and records the outcome with its rationale in the credit file. External information is used, including the Dutch and German credit registers, Chamber of Commerce filings, the Graydon and Creditreform credit alerts, sector outlooks and press reports. For each indicator the identification method, sources, monitoring frequency and responsibilities are laid down in the corporate UTP procedure WCR-P-031, and the watchlist and forborne exposure lists are reviewed monthly. Because UTP decisions are expert-based, FR&R applies a labelling guideline with worked examples and performs an annual consistency review of UTP decisions across credit teams; the 2025 review found no systematic differences between teams (UTP share 41–46% of defaults per team). Technical past due situations are recognised only in the cases listed in EBA/GL/2016/07, corrected within 30 days, and the 41 technical past due events are removed from the RDS default events.

sections.heading: Data sources
sections.text: The RDS combines the corporate rating tool CorpRate (ratings, qualitative answers, overrides, rating dates and raters since 2014) and its predecessor RateWise (2007–2014), the spreading tool FinSpread (financial statements), the loan administration system LoanIQ (exposures, limits, arrears), the default register DefaultHub and the watchlist and forbearance registers. Each source belongs to a data domain with exactly one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue (Wholesale Lending, Credit Risk Data, Wholesale Credit Operations), and the authoritative source of each data type is defined: CorpRate for ratings, FinSpread for financial statements, LoanIQ for exposures and DefaultHub for defaults. Common obligors across sources are identified with the Group counterparty identifier, so each obligor is counted only once in the one-year default rates even where it holds exposures in several legal entities. sections.heading: Lineage and critical data elements
sections.text: Lineage from the source systems to the RDS is documented for every variable in RDS Annex A, including source table and field, intermediate stores, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build code, and extraction frequency and timing; discarded variables used to construct retained variables (for example the raw balance sheet items behind the seven ratios) are included. For the external ratings the lineage starts at receipt in the market data platform and records the provider, the data product and the delivery date. All model input variables and the elements of the target (default flag, default date, obligor scope flags) are critical data elements with business and technical definitions and DQ rules per applicable dimension. The only manual steps are the version-controlled mapping of RateWise industry codes to NACE Rev. 2 and the list of wrongly scoped obligors identified by Wholesale Credit Operations; both are identified in the lineage with their four-eyes control and documented as expert judgement. The lineage was updated in October 2025 for the migration of LoanIQ to the cloud platform before those data were used, and the Data Owners confirmed that changes to definitions or transformations will be approved by them and communicated in advance.

sections.heading: Rating histories and timing of risk drivers
sections.text: For every obligor the RDS stores the complete rating history: rating dates, model version, score, grade before and after override, override reason, qualitative answers, the financial statement used and the rater and approver, as well as the identity and date and circumstances of each default and the PD and realised default rate per grade. Risk drivers are taken as they were available at each reference date: the financial ratios from the latest financial statement available at that date (not the statement of the reference year), and the qualitative answers from the latest approved rating; for defaulted obligors the values are therefore available throughout the year before default. The median age of the financial statement at the reference date is 9 months; 6.8% of obligor-quarters use a statement older than 18 months and 2.9% one older than 24 months, which is treated in the model as described in MDD section 4.5. Loan-by-loan data, including the ratings, overrides and credit-granting criteria applied at origination, are captured in CorpRate and LoanIQ so that deviations, exceptions and overrides can be tracked.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Each exclusion is documented with its reason, number of observations, share and defaults, and was approved by the Model Owner on 5 February 2026 (ticket WCRM-3318): X1 – obligors wrongly assigned to the model scope at the reference date (revenue outside EUR 25–500 million after correction, financial institutions, specialised lending), 9,850 obligor-quarters (2.4%) and 18 defaults, removed from numerator and denominator; X2 – technical past due default events, 41 events, removed from the numerator only because they were wrongly classified as defaults. Obligors without any on- or off-balance-sheet credit obligation at the start of the period are not part of the default rate denominator by definition (6,120 obligor-quarters, 1.5%). Obligors without a valid rating at the start of a period (3,480 obligor-quarters, 0.8%, default rate 3.9%) are not excluded: they are included in the portfolio-level default rates and analysed separately. Obligors that migrate to another model or approach, repay or whose loans are sold or written off during the year remain in the one-year default rate of their cohort; the resulting bias was analysed and is negligible (effect on the LRA below 0.01 percentage points). No exclusion exceeds 5% of observations or exposure in any segment, and the conclusions of the impact analysis are given in section 5.3.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in RDS Annex C: financial ratios missing for a structural reason (for example interest coverage for obligors without interest-bearing debt, 3.1%) receive the value of the best bucket, and ratios missing because of a data deficiency (1.8%) receive the bucket with the highest observed default rate, in development and production alike. The share of imputed values per variable is reported in Annex C (maximum 4.4% for revenue growth), and re-estimating the financial module without the imputed observations changes no coefficient by more than 6%. Outliers of financial ratios are identified with documented percentile criteria and winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles of the development sample; the same caps are stored in the CorpRate parameter table and applied in production, and the effect of capping on the AUC is below 0.002. The default flag and default date are never imputed; 12 events with unclear default dates were resolved with FR&R from the credit files.

sections.heading: Construction of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated for each of the 68 quarterly reference dates using overlapping one-year windows: the denominator comprises obligors in scope with a credit obligation and not in default at the reference date, the numerator those among them with at least one default in the following twelve months. Grades at the start of each window are the final grades after override, without substitution effects of guarantees or ex post conservative adjustments. The same exclusion and adjustment rules are applied to the calibration data, the monitoring data and the data used in the annual review of estimates. The calibration sample per reference date and grade is stored in the frozen RDS (table calib_sample) and described in MDD section 5.2.

sections.heading: Representativeness – scope and risk drivers
sections.text: Representativeness is assessed under the Bank's representativeness policy (CRM-STD-100 §6.5 and MV-HB-003 §6), which specifies the PSI per risk driver and score, with green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25 and red above 0.25, and a two-sample test of default rates, separately for the development data of the modules and for the calibration data. The scope of the RDS equals the current range of application; against the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 (6,880 obligors), the PSI is 0.05 for the score, below 0.10 for six of the seven financial ratios and all qualitative questions, and 0.13 for revenue growth, which is explained by the inflation-driven nominal revenue growth of 2022–2024 and does not affect the ranking. Missing-value shares are 1.9% in the RDS and 1.4% in the application portfolio.

sections.heading: Representativeness – default rate levels, lending standards and economic conditions
sections.text: Representativeness of default rate levels: the 2023–2024 one-year default rates (1.1% and 1.3%) do not differ significantly from the RDS rates for the same grades (two-sample test of proportions per grade, no significant difference at 5% for 19 of 20 grades), and the current portfolio's average grade is similar to that of the RDS. The change of lending standards in 2014 was analysed by comparing RDS data before and after: default rates of construction and real estate development obligors were 2.1 times those of other sectors in 2008–2013 and 1.5 times afterwards; because the model's sector outlook question and the financial ratios capture most of this difference, no separate adjustment was made, and the remaining uncertainty is covered by MoC category B (B-01). Recovery policies and the legal environment (Dutch insolvency law, including the WHOA restructuring procedure introduced in 2021) were assessed; WHOA restructurings are treated as distressed restructurings and are reflected in the 2021–2024 data. Economic conditions in the RDS include severe recession years and are relevant to current and foreseeable conditions.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The impact of each exclusion on the long-run average default rate and on the risk driver distributions was quantified: X1 changes the LRA by +0.02 percentage points (the excluded obligors have a lower default rate), X2 by −0.05 percentage points, and the combined effect of all exclusions is −0.03 percentage points (−2% relative). The PSI of the score between the RDS before and after exclusions is below 0.01, and the grade distribution is unchanged, so the exclusions do not affect representativeness.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The DQ assessment was performed in January 2026 against the dimensions of MRM-STD-022 and is reported in the data quality assessment EVD-06-DQ; all critical data elements are within their thresholds except the completeness of qualitative answers for 2008–2013 (RateWise stored only the module score for 11% of ratings, amber) and the timeliness of financial statements (2.9% older than 24 months, amber). The RDS reconciles to the exposures in LoanIQ and to the finance ledger (difference 0.04% of drawn amounts at year-ends), and the default events to the default register. The assessment concludes that the RDS is fit for the recalibration of PD-CORP-MM v3.1 and for the review of the risk differentiation modules, and was signed off by the developer and the Model Owner on 30 January 2026 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: The data deficiency log records each deficiency with identifier, affected period and variables, DQ dimension, cause, impact, treatment, owner and target date, and each open deficiency is cross-referenced to the MDD limitations log and its MoC category. DD-PD-01 – default flag reconstructed for 2008–2015 (all grades; accuracy): default rates understated by about 2.5% relative; MoC A-01; permanent; limitation L-01. DD-PD-02 – qualitative answers missing for 11% of RateWise ratings 2008–2013 (qualitative module; completeness): module score used instead of the answers; affects only the re-test of the qualitative weights, not the calibration; no MoC; closed as permanent. DD-PD-03 – financial statements older than 24 months for 2.9% of observations (financial module; timeliness): treated in the model by the notching rule of MDD section 4.5; MoC A-02; owner Wholesale Credit Operations for the timely collection of statements, target date 31 December 2026; limitation L-03. sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: PD-CORP-MM (the Corporate Rating Model) assigns an obligor rating on the Bank's non-retail master scale and a one-year probability of default to mid-market corporate clients; version 3.1 is the annual recalibration of version 3.0, which received ECB permission as a material change on 18 September 2024 and went live on 1 December 2024. Intended uses are the calculation of own funds requirements for the corporate exposure class under the IRB approach and the credit approval process (the rating is mandatory for every credit decision and determines the approval authority); secondary uses are IFRS 9 staging, risk-adjusted pricing, limit setting, economic capital and the early warning process. Users are the account managers and credit analysts of Wholesale Banking (rating proposals), Credit Risk Management (rating approval and credit decisions), Capital Management, Finance – Impairments and Wholesale Pricing. Cover block: title MDD Corporate Rating Model; model PD-CORP-MM v3.1 (MDL-06); document version 0.9; status draft for review; author A. Hoekstra; reviewer L. Meijer; approvers P. van Dijk (Model Owner) and T. Kramer (Head of Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling); not yet approved.

sections.heading: Range of application
sections.text: The range of application comprises non-financial corporates with consolidated annual revenue from EUR 25 million up to EUR 500 million (6,940 obligors, EAD EUR 16.8 billion, RWEA EUR 9.1 billion at 30 June 2026), booked in the Netherlands and the German and Belgian branches; groups are rated at the level of each obligor, with group support assessed as described in section 4.4. Corporates with revenue above EUR 500 million are rated by the large corporate model and their LGD and CCF are treated under the Foundation IRB approach; specialised lending and financial institutions are outside the range of application. All exposures of the corporate exposure class are under the IRB approach; the only permanent partial use is the corporate portfolio of the Luxembourg subsidiary (43 obligors, EAD EUR 0.2 billion), immaterial in size and risk profile under CRR Article 150(1), whose share of the corporate EAD (0.6%) is monitored quarterly against the 2% trigger of the roll-out plan. The roll-out plan for the corporate exposure class has been completed, and exposures are assigned to exposure classes by the documented assignment routine, applied in the same sequence since 2018.

sections.heading: Use in credit processes and internal parameters
sections.text: Ratings and PDs play an essential role in the Bank's credit processes: no credit is granted, renewed or restructured without a valid approved rating; the rating and exposure determine the approval authority (business-line authority up to grade C12 and EUR 10 million, Credit Risk Management above, Group Credit Committee for grades C17–C20 or above EUR 75 million); and the PD is used in pricing, limit setting, the credit risk appetite (EL and RWA density), internal capital allocation to Wholesale Banking and quarterly management reporting. The credit approval framework, including the approval authorities and the role of the rating, is laid down in the Credit Risk Policy CR-POL-001 approved by the Management Board. Credit decisions are never fully automated for corporates: the model output supports the creditworthiness assessment, and every decision is taken by authorised decision-makers under the four-eyes principle with independent approval by Credit Risk Management above the business-line authority, as required by CR-POL-001 §5.2 and §5.3. For IFRS 9 the PD is converted to a point-in-time, forward-looking lifetime PD without MoC in model MDL-08, and pricing uses the best-estimate PD without MoC; these differences are documented in the parameter mapping table PMT-PD-2026 and justified by the different purposes. All parameters used in the credit risk appetite metrics for mid-market corporates come from models registered in the inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Tier, inventory record and regulatory status
sections.text: The model is registered in the model inventory as MDL-06 with version 3.1 recorded at gate G0 on 3 November 2025 (change log entry CHG-2025-131); the inventory states name, version, purpose, uses, scope, risk type, regulatory use (IRB PD corporates), model family (statistical), Model Owner P. van Dijk (Director Wholesale Credit Risk), developer Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling, main users and the validation team Model Validation – Credit Risk. The model is Tier 1: materiality High (RWEA EUR 9.1 billion, 29% of credit risk RWEA; used in credit decisions) and complexity Medium (two modules, expert-weighted qualitative module, notching and overrides), which gives Tier 1 in the matrix of MRM-STD-010 §6.4; the tier was confirmed at the initial validation of v3.0 and at the annual tier review of 14 October 2025. The inventory records the AI Act classification (statistical model with fixed logic, not an AI system), that no personal data are processed, the supervisory permission of 18 September 2024 with its two obligations, the latest validation opinion (fit for purpose, annual validation 2025, report of 28 November 2025), open findings, limitations and the lifecycle stage; the Model Owner updates it within ten business days of changes and attests it quarterly. The rating system is classified as material in the Bank's IRB materiality assessment, which is communicated annually to the ECB, and management reporting on the rating system covers its materiality, strengths, limitations and validation and audit status.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system consists of clearly separated components: (a) a financial module, a logistic regression on seven financial ratios; (b) a qualitative module of eight questions; (c) the combination of both module scores into a rating score; (d) automatic notching for warning signals, outdated financial statements and group support; (e) the calibration of the score to a best-estimate PD and the assignment to the master scale; (f) the margin of conservatism; (g) the PD floor; and (h) the override process. The model follows a shadow-rating design in which the business risk profile (qualitative module) and the financial risk profile (financial module) are combined in the way rating agencies assess corporates; the qualitative weights were derived partly from external ratings (section 4.3), whereas the financial module and the calibration are based on the Bank's own default experience. The model is developed in-house; no vendor model or proprietary technology is used. The documentation of the rating process, the rating tool manual CorpRate v3 and the implementation specification allow a third party to understand, replicate and evaluate the assignment of obligors to grades.

sections.heading: Rating philosophy
sections.text: The model follows the Bank's hybrid rating philosophy: the financial ratios and the sector outlook and account conduct questions make grade assignment responsive to current obligor-specific and economic conditions, while the PD per grade is calibrated to the long-run average default rate. The expected dynamics are moderate grade migration over the cycle (in 2009 and 2020 the average grade deteriorated by 0.9 and 0.6 notches) and grade-level default rates that rise in downturns; the observed migration and yearly default rates per grade over 2008–2024 are consistent with this philosophy, as analysed in section 7.4. The rating scale reflects exclusively the risk of obligor default; facility characteristics such as collateral are not part of the rating.

sections.heading: Rating assignment process
sections.text: The account manager or credit analyst prepares the rating in CorpRate, including the financial statements spread in FinSpread and the qualitative answers with written justification; the rating is approved by a credit risk officer in Credit Risk Management who does not benefit from the credit decision. Ratings are reviewed at least annually, at least semi-annually for watchlist obligors, and whenever material new information becomes available (new financial statements, warning signals, restructuring); no new credit is granted to an obligor with a rating older than 12 months. The rating criteria, questions and answer guidelines are set out in the rating manual and applied identically in the Netherlands and the branches, so obligors with similar risk are assigned consistently to the same grade. All relevant and current information is considered in the rating: financial statements, management accounts, qualitative information and external information from credit registers and credit bureaux; where information is limited (for example outdated statements), the rating is more conservative. Where the credit officer has concerns about the accuracy of the information provided, reasonable enquiries and verification with the borrower and third parties are performed and documented before the rating is approved.

sections.heading: Dependencies and stress testing
sections.text: The model depends on the default register (target) and on FinSpread (inputs); its PDs are used by the corporate LGD model (MDL-07) for expected loss and by the IFRS 9 PD model (MDL-08). In the ICAAP and the EBA and internal stress tests, the rating grades are migrated with a satellite model linking grade migrations to GDP and sector variables, and the effect on own funds requirements of the severe but plausible recession scenario of the 2026 ICAAP was an RWEA increase of 14.2% for the range of application, reported to the Management Board with the ICAAP. The model complexity was assessed as Medium in the regular complexity assessment of MRM (October 2025); the model is not highly complex and not dynamic.

sections.heading: Reference data set and samples
sections.text: The model is recalibrated on the frozen RDS RDS-PDCORP-3.1 described in the approved RDS documentation EVD-06-RDS version 1.0 of 13 February 2026: 412,600 obligor-quarter observations with reference dates 2008–2024 and 1,386 default events. Data deficiencies DD-PD-01 and DD-PD-03 are carried into the limitations log and the MoC register. The calibration sample is the full RDS for all 68 reference dates, after the exclusions of RDS section 4.2; it is stored in the frozen RDS (table calib_sample) with 6,068 obligors per reference date on average. For the development of v3.0 in 2022 the samples were defined before estimation: development sample with reference dates 2008–2018 (70% random obligor split), out-of-sample the remaining 30% of obligors, and out-of-time sample reference dates 2019–2020; the out-of-time sample was not used for driver selection or estimation. For v3.1 the module coefficients were not re-estimated; their performance was re-tested on the post-development period 2021–2024 (99,800 obligor-quarters, 283 defaults), which serves as an additional out-of-time sample.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives, selection and selection bias
sections.text: For v3.0 four approaches were compared against regulatory compliance, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation criteria: (A) a two-module scorecard with logistic regression (selected), (B) a single logistic regression on financial and qualitative variables, (C) a pure shadow-rating model regressing agency-implied PDs on all drivers, and (D) a gradient boosting model. C was rejected because only 612 obligors (5% of the RDS) have an external rating and they are larger than the typical mid-market client; B performed comparably to A (out-of-time AUC 0.812 against 0.816) but mixed qualitative and financial information in a way credit officers found hard to challenge; D reached an out-of-time AUC of 0.846 but was rejected because of limited interpretability for credit decisions and the controls it would require. The selection of the less complex approach A is justified because its interpretability supports the use in credit decisions and challenge by credit officers; the gradient boosting model is retained as challenger (section 7.5). The model is applied to existing clients and prospects; declined prospects are few (4.2% of rated prospects in 2019–2024) and are rated with the same tool, so reject inference was not performed. The omission is justified by an analysis of the 214 declined prospects since 2019 that were subsequently financed by other banks: their default rate (2.8%) is in line with their assigned grades (average PD 2.6%), showing that selection bias has an immaterial effect on ranking.

sections.heading: Financial module
sections.text: The long list of 42 candidate ratios was compiled from literature, rating agency methodologies and the credit analysts of Wholesale Banking, and the expected sign of each ratio was stated before estimation. Variable selection combined univariate AUC and monotonicity tests, stability of the univariate AUC over the years, exclusion of one of each pair of ratios with a rank correlation above 0.6, and stepwise logistic regression with expert review of the candidate sets. The final seven ratios and their relative weights are: interest coverage (21%), net debt / EBITDA (19%), equity ratio (18%), return on assets (14%), current ratio (10%), log revenue (9%) and revenue growth (9%); all signs are as expected (higher coverage, equity, profitability, liquidity, size and growth lower the PD; higher leverage raises it) and all coefficients are significant at 1%. The ratios are available for every obligor at the point of use from the latest financial statement and were stable over the development period (yearly univariate AUC range below 0.08). The financial module has an AUC of 0.781 on the development sample.

sections.heading: Qualitative module and shadow-rating calibration of its weights
sections.text: The qualitative module contains eight questions with four to five answer categories: market position, management and governance, business model sustainability, customer and supplier concentration, sector outlook, financial flexibility, quality of financial reporting and account conduct. The weights were derived in two steps: a regression of the logit of the agency-implied one-year PD on the answers for the 612 externally rated obligors (R² 0.58), followed by a review by an expert panel of eight senior credit officers in May 2022, which increased the weight of account conduct from 8% to 12% and reduced market position from 18% to 14% because the internal default data showed stronger discriminatory power of account conduct; the panel and its elicitation are documented in EVD-06-EJ. The module has an AUC of 0.724 on internal defaults and its final weights were tested against the purely statistical weights, which give an AUC of 0.731; the impact of the expert adjustment on model performance is therefore small and was accepted in favour of interpretability.

sections.heading: Combination, warning signals and group support
sections.text: The module scores are combined in a logistic regression on internal defaults, giving weights of 64% to the financial and 36% to the qualitative module; the combined score has an AUC of 0.832 on the development sample. Warning signals lead to automatic downgrades of the grade after the score: financial covenant breach in the last 12 months (one notch), payment arrears above 30 days in the last three months (two notches), negative equity (two notches) and an adverse or disclaimed audit opinion (one notch), with a maximum cumulative downgrade of four notches; these rules reflect information not fully captured by the modules. Group support: where a stronger parent is assessed to provide strong or moderate support under the documented support assessment, the grade is improved by up to two or one notch respectively, never above the parent's grade. The notching rules were set by expert judgement (EJ-PD-03) and their impact was quantified: warning signal downgrades affect 7.4% of obligors and increase the AUC from 0.829 to 0.832; group support uplifts affect 4.1% of obligors and do not change the AUC.

sections.heading: Outdated financial statements
sections.text: Where the latest financial statement used in the rating is older than 18 months at the rating date, the tool applies a one-notch downgrade, and where it is older than 24 months a two-notch downgrade; ratings based on statements older than 36 months cannot be approved. The two-notch adjustment was chosen because obligors with statements older than 24 months had a default rate of 3.1% in 2016–2024, about two grades worse than their unadjusted average grade (C11, grade PD 0.98%) would imply; it is recorded as expert judgement EJ-PD-04 and supported by the sensitivity analysis in section 7.6. The remaining uncertainty is covered by MoC A-02.

sections.heading: Calibration target and long-run average default rate
sections.text: The PD is calibrated for one calibration segment, the whole range of application, to the long-run average of one-year default rates calculated quarterly with overlapping windows as the arithmetic average of the count-based default rates of the 68 reference dates 2008–2024; exposure weighting is not used. The observed average default rate is 1.55%; the default rates of 2020 and 2021 were strongly reduced by government support (GDP −3.9% in 2020 but default rate 1.6%), so, to reflect the likely range of variability, the one-year default rates of the eight reference dates in 2020–2021 were replaced by the rates predicted by the regression of default rates on GDP growth estimated on 2008–2019 (2.4% and 1.5%), which raises the LRA to 1.66%. The adjustment is an upward adjustment and is documented as expert judgement EJ-PD-05. Where the LRA falls below the higher of the five-year and all-data averages, the Bank would justify it; this is not the case, since the five-year average (2020–2024, 1.15% observed) is lower than the LRA.

sections.heading: Calibration method
sections.text: The combined score is transformed into a best-estimate PD with a logistic calibration function whose slope is retained from development (slope test on 2021–2024 data: 0.97, not significantly different from 1, p = 0.41) and whose intercept is set so that the average best-estimate PD over the calibration sample, after notching and overrides, equals the LRA of 1.66%. The calibration is performed on final grades after overrides and before the MoC and the regulatory floor, and it is monotone, so it does not change the rank ordering of obligors within the segment. Continuous PDs are used only to assign obligors to the master scale; the PD applied for own funds is the grade PD, and no smoothing is used to compensate for lack of data or low discriminatory power. The estimates are based on the Bank's historical default experience and empirical evidence of all relevant data, and are derived from the long-run average, not from judgement alone.

sections.heading: Master scale mapping, floors and grade distribution
sections.text: Each obligor is assigned by its best-estimate PD to one of the 20 non-defaulted grades C01–C20 of the Bank's non-retail master scale (plus default grade D), which exceeds the seven non-defaulted grades required by CRR Article 170(1)(b); each grade maps to exactly one master scale grade and grade PDs increase monotonically. Final grade PDs after MoC are, for example, C05 0.14%, C08 0.38%, C10 0.72%, C12 1.35%, C14 2.62%, C16 5.20%, C18 11.5% and C20 31.0%. The PD applied to each exposure is at least 0.05% in accordance with CRR Article 160(1); the floor is applied after the MoC and is binding for grades C01 and C02 (1.9% of obligors, 3.2% of EAD). 88% of obligors are in grades C06–C14; the largest grade (C10) holds 13.8% of obligors, below the 30% limit of CRM-STD-100 §5.4, and the portfolio's concentration in the middle of the scale is covered by enough grades with narrow PD bands.

sections.heading: Calibration tests
sections.text: Calibration tests were performed per grade and for the segment with the one-sided Jeffreys test and the exact binomial test of the grade PD (best estimate) against the observed default rates of the full calibration sample, and for each LRA calculation date the average best-estimate PD was compared with the one-year default rate and with the LRA. Results: portfolio p-value 0.47; one grade (C13) with p < 5% and none with p < 1%, which is within the green thresholds; the qualitative analysis confirms at least 20 obligors in every grade, no excessive concentration and a unimodal obligor distribution. The calibration therefore provides accurate and consistent quantitative estimates at grade level.

sections.heading: MoC framework and identification of deficiencies
sections.text: The MoC follows CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 section 4.4: the final PD is the best estimate after appropriate adjustments plus a MoC for category A (data and methodological deficiencies), category B (relevant changes) and category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 in the recalibration, including those raised by the 2025 annual validation; for each, an appropriate adjustment was considered first (the COVID-19 adjustment of the LRA is such an adjustment), and the MoC is not used for deficiencies that can be corrected. Deficiencies considered and rejected: the RateWise-to-CorpRate migration in 2014 (no effect on the calibration data), the missing qualitative answers 2008–2013 (affects only the module re-test) and the WHOA procedure (already reflected in the data).

sections.heading: MoC category A
sections.text: A-01 (default flag reconstruction 2008–2015, DD-PD-01): the LRA was re-estimated under three treatments of the P1 period (as reconstructed; P1 default rates increased by the 2.5% relative understatement estimated on P3 data; P1 default rates increased by the 3.9% missed-default rate without deduction of false defaults); the adverse effect ranges from +0.02 to +0.04 percentage points on the LRA, and the MoC is set at 2.4% of the grade PDs (+0.04 percentage points on average). A-02 (outdated financial statements, DD-PD-03): the notching rule of section 4.5 was compared with alternatives (one notch, three notches, grade-specific notching); the adverse effect on the portfolio average PD is +0.02 percentage points, set as MoC of 1.2% of the grade PDs. A-02 has a remediation plan (timely collection of statements, owner Wholesale Credit Operations, 31 December 2026); A-01 is permanent and reassessed annually.

sections.text: B-01 (change in lending standards in 2014): because the sector mix of the RDS before 2014 differs from the current portfolio, the LRA was recomputed with the 2008–2013 default rates re-weighted to the current sector mix and, alternatively, with 2008–2013 excluded (plausible range of the effect on the LRA −0.03 to +0.05 percentage points); the MoC is set at 3.0% of the grade PDs (+0.05 percentage points), equal to the upper end of the range. B-02 (COVID-19 support measures, affecting the 2020–2021 default rates): the appropriate adjustment of section 5.1 corrects the bias; its uncertainty (confidence interval of the regression prediction) corresponds to +0.03 percentage points, set as MoC of 1.8% of the grade PDs.

sections.heading: MoC category C
sections.text: Category C MoC is the difference between the upper bound of a one-sided 90% confidence interval of the LRA default rate and the LRA, computed with the variance of yearly default rates adjusted for their first-order autocorrelation (0.52): the upper bound is 1.75%, giving +0.09 percentage points or 5.4% of the LRA. At grade level the category C MoC is based on the distribution of the grade-level default rate estimator and therefore increases for grades with fewer observations: from 4.8% of the PD in C10 to 11.9% in C20.

sections.heading: MoC aggregation, register and effect
sections.text: The total MoC per grade is the sum of categories A, B and C without diversification; at portfolio level A is 3.6%, B 4.8% and C 5.4% of the best estimate, 13.8% in total (+0.23 percentage points), giving a portfolio-average final PD of 1.89% before floors. The MoC is applied multiplicatively per grade to the calibrated best-estimate grade PD before the floor, which preserves rank ordering: PDs after MoC increase monotonically with grade. The MoC register MOC-REG-MDL06 lists every deficiency with category, affected component and grades, quantification method, MoC value and remediation status, and the MDD documents the complete list of deficiencies with their category and methods. The total MoC is below 20% of the best estimate, so no redevelopment assessment is required under CRM-STD-101 §7.2. The MoC increases RWEA by EUR 312 million (A 82, B 109, C 121), reported per category in the quarterly MoC report, and MoC levels are reviewed in the annual review of estimates; a component is reduced only after confirmed remediation, and MoC changes are classified as model changes.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: The AUC of the combined rating (after notching and overrides) is 0.832 (Gini 0.664) on the development sample, 0.824 out-of-sample, 0.816 on the 2019–2020 out-of-time sample and 0.809 (Gini 0.618) on the 2021–2024 re-test sample, with a 95% DeLong confidence interval of 0.785–0.833 for the latter. The relative decrease of the Gini coefficient against development is 6.9%, which is green under the 10% and 20% thresholds, and the Gini is well above the red threshold of 0.45 for corporate PD models. By country the AUC on 2021–2024 is 0.812 (Netherlands), 0.794 (Germany) and 0.801 (Belgium), and by size class between 0.79 and 0.82.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: Realised default rates were compared with the grade PDs for every year 2008–2024: the rank ordering of default rates by grade holds in every year, grade-level default rates rise in 2009, 2012–2013 and fall in 2017–2019 and 2021–2022, and in each year at most three grades show a default rate outside the 95% Jeffreys interval of the best-estimate PD. On the 2021–2024 sample the observed default rate (1.02%) is below the average best-estimate PD (1.49%), which reflects the benign period and the support measures, not an overestimation of the long-run average. All performance metrics are within their thresholds, so no limitation had to be logged under MRM-STD-020 §8.3.

sections.heading: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of grades
sections.text: Heterogeneity: the default rates of adjacent grades differ significantly (one-sided test at 5%) for 17 of the 19 adjacent pairs; the exceptions are C01/C02 and C02/C03, which have very few defaults and are kept because they are needed for the large obligors near the floor; there are no significant overlaps of default risk between grades. Homogeneity: within each grade, the default rates of subsets by country, sector group, size class and financial statement age were tested against the rest of the grade; no subset with at least 200 obligor-quarters differs significantly after Bonferroni correction, except obligors with statements older than 24 months in grades C09–C12, which are addressed by the notching rule. The rating system therefore differentiates risk meaningfully and groups obligors with similar default risk.

sections.heading: Stability and rating migration
sections.text: The PSI of the score between the development sample and the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 is 0.05; the twelve-month migration matrix for 2025 shows 71% of obligors within one notch and 6.4% migrating by more than two grades. The upper and lower matrix weighted bandwidths are 0.43 and 0.39 (v3.0 initial validation: 0.40 and 0.37), and the pairwise z-tests of off-diagonal transition frequencies show no significant non-monotonicity. The Herfindahl index of the grade distribution is 0.071, with no significant change of its coefficient of variation against the initial validation. Design stability was tested by re-estimating the financial module on reference dates 2012–2020 and 2016–2024: all coefficients keep their sign and differ by less than 25% from the development coefficients.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key choices: LRA window (2008–2018 only 1.81%; without the COVID-19 adjustment 1.55%), notching for outdated statements (one notch: portfolio PD −0.4%; three notches: +0.3%), qualitative weights (statistical instead of expert weights: AUC +0.001, RWEA −0.6%), warning-signal notching removed (RWEA −1.9%) and group support removed (RWEA +2.3%). The results are documented with their effect on the model output and were used to support the MoC quantification in chapter 6. The sensitivity analysis also shows the circumstances in which the model is less reliable (section 8.3).

sections.heading: Climate-related and environmental risks
sections.text: Climate-related and environmental risks were assessed for materiality in the 2025 annual review using the Bank's sector heatmap: 18% of the EAD is in sectors with high transition risk (transport, chemicals, agriculture), and the sector outlook question of the qualitative module was extended in v3.0 with guidance to consider transition risk; no additional climate driver was included because the default data show no significant effect after controlling for the existing drivers (p = 0.37). The assessment will be repeated at each annual review.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: Material assumptions are: (1) the relationship between financial ratios and default is stable over time; (2) the qualitative answers are applied consistently by credit analysts; (3) the 2020–2021 default rates understate the risk of those economic conditions because of support measures; (4) the current sector mix will remain; and (5) the notching rules adequately compensate for information not in the modules. Assumption 1 is supported by the stability tests in section 7.4, assumption 2 by the consistency reviews of rating quality by Credit Risk Management, assumption 3 by the GDP regression, and assumptions 4 and 5 by the sensitivity analyses and the MoC.

sections.heading: Circumstances in which the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The model is not suitable for start-ups without two years of financial statements, holding companies without operations, project and object finance, public sector entities and corporates in financial restructuring; such obligors are rated with the specialised tools or the expert module and the rating manual prohibits the use of PD-CORP-MM for them. The model may underestimate risk where financial statements are outdated or in very rapid sector shocks not yet visible in the statements; the warning signals and overrides mitigate this.
