sections.heading: Implementation specification, handover and production controls
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-PDCORP-3.1 (approved by the Model Owner on 9 March 2026) is consistent with this MDD and defines inputs, source fields and lineage, ratio definitions, caps, missing value rules, coefficients, notching rules, calibration function, master scale mapping, MoC factors, PD floor, override rules and rounding. The handover package contained the specification, the parameter file params_v3.1.0.json, 2,400 test cases with expected outputs from the development code, including boundary, missing and invalid inputs and every grade, and reference outputs for the portfolio at 31 December 2025. Implementation testing, the reconciliation with the development outputs and the parallel run are performed by the PD engine team and Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling and documented in the implementation and testing report EVD-06-IMPL. All parameters of CorpRate and of the PD engine (coefficients, caps, calibration function, master scale, MoC factors, notching rules) are version-controlled parameter tables with restricted access, changed only through the model change and approval process; model developers have no write access to production. Each rating stores the model and parameter version used, and the monthly PD engine run logs reference date, input data version, code version and parameter version.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan – KPIs, frequency and responsibilities
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-PDCORP-3.1 is approved by the Model Owner and reviewed by Model Validation; it defines the KPIs and their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference periods, segments (country and size class), responsible persons and escalation. KPIs are PSI of score, grades and drivers, AUC/Gini on the latest one-year window, Jeffreys and binomial tests per grade and portfolio, migration and concentration statistics, override rates by direction, reason, magnitude and approving unit, overlays, production data quality and model coverage (share of obligors with a valid rating and share of outdated ratings). Monitoring is quarterly for the Tier 1 model, with calibration KPIs on rolling one-year windows; reports are finalised within 60 days after quarter-end and show value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four quarters, and the monitoring code is version-controlled (tag mon-v3.1.0) so results are reproducible. The plan is updated with every model change and reviewed at least annually; it was last updated for v3.1 in March 2026.

sections.heading: Monitoring thresholds and escalation
sections.text: Thresholds: PSI green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25; relative Gini decrease above 10% amber and above 20% red, and a Gini below 0.40 red regardless of change; calibration amber if the portfolio p-value is below 5% or more than 20% of grades are below 5%, red if the portfolio p-value is below 1% or more than 30% of grades are below 1%; override rate above 10% amber and above 20% red. Amber results are analysed by the Model Owner; a red result or two consecutive ambers on the same KPI are notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 days proposing no action, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use; red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the MRC. A red outcome leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the MRC within three months, and results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and an additional MoC. Monitoring results are sent to Credit Risk Management, which uses them in the credit risk reporting and in the review of the credit approval framework.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates
sections.text: The framework for the regular review of estimates defines the minimum scope, frequency, metrics, thresholds and significance levels, and the actions for adverse results: at least annually and whenever new information comes to light, the review analyses the representativeness of the RDS against the application portfolio, model performance and its stability on the whole application portfolio per period against development, and predictive power, including whether recent data change the LRA materially, with back-testing per grade. Predictive power is analysed at grade level with the Jeffreys and binomial tests, the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and charts of default rates against PDs per grade. The annual model review also covers portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the Model Owner and is provided to MRM and Model Validation. The 2025 review (report of 30 October 2025) concluded that the model remains fit for purpose and that the annual recalibration documented here was required, including the extension of the data window with 2024; the MoC for the reconstructed default flag was reassessed with the longer P3 period. Where realised default rates exceed the grade PDs beyond the red threshold in two consecutive annual reviews, taking the cycle into account, the PDs are revised upward; methods and data are kept consistent over time and any change is documented in the review report.

sections.heading: Override policy, monitoring and performance
sections.text: Overrides of the model grade are permitted only on the basis of relevant information not captured by the model, using the closed list of nine reason codes of the rating manual (for example imminent loss of a key contract, pending litigation, unaudited recent figures showing material change, parental support not captured by the notching rule). Each override is documented in CorpRate with reason code, written rationale, supporting evidence, proposer and approver, and is approved by Credit Risk Management independently of the proposer; the default grade D and the fraud warning signal cannot be overridden. The maximum override is three notches; upward overrides are more restricted than downward overrides: upward overrides of more than two notches require approval by the Group Credit Committee, and upward overrides may not exceed 5% of ratings per quarter, while downward overrides may be approved by any credit risk officer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly by country, reason and approving unit; rates above 10% are analysed by the Model Owner and reported to MRM. The performance of overrides is analysed annually: in 2016–2024 the default rate of downward-overridden obligors was 2.9% against 1.4% for their pre-override grades and 3.0% for their final grades, and that of upward-overridden obligors 0.9% against 1.2% pre-override; the overrides therefore improve discriminatory power (AUC 0.829 before and 0.832 after overrides). Systematic overrides would be treated as an indication of model deficiency; the most frequent reason (unaudited recent figures, 31% of overrides) is addressed by the monitoring of statement age.

sections.heading: Change classification and regulatory status
sections.text: The recalibration updates the LRA with the latest data, re-quantifies the MoC with the existing methodology and leaves methodology, drivers, rating philosophy, default definition and range of application unchanged; it is therefore not internally material, and under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 it is a non-material change notified ex post (Class C). The impact was computed on 31 December 2025 on the same exposures before and after the change: RWEA of the range of application −0.9% and Bank-wide credit RWEA −0.26%, below the 5% and 1.5% thresholds, and 8.1% of obligors change grade, below the 10% threshold of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e). MRM confirmed the classification on 24 November 2025; the change, planned for implementation on 1 April 2026, will be included in the ex post notification to the ECB for the second quarter of 2026, with description, rationale, implementation date, scope, internal approval and impact. The two obligations of the ECB permission of 2024 (monitoring of the override rate and reassessment of the COVID-19 treatment in the LRA) are recorded in the inventory with owner and deadline and tracked as MRC conditions; this recalibration addresses the second obligation.

sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: PD-CORP-MM (the Corporate Rating Model) assigns an obligor rating on the Bank's non-retail master scale and a one-year probability of default to mid-market corporate clients; version 3.1 is the annual recalibration of version 3.0, which received ECB permission as a material change on 18 September 2024 and went live on 1 December 2024. Intended uses are the calculation of own funds requirements for the corporate exposure class under the IRB approach and the credit approval process (the rating is mandatory for every credit decision and determines the approval authority); secondary uses are IFRS 9 staging, risk-adjusted pricing, limit setting, economic capital and the early warning process. Users are the account managers and credit analysts of Wholesale Banking (rating proposals), Credit Risk Management (rating approval and credit decisions), Capital Management, Finance – Impairments and Wholesale Pricing. sections.heading: Range of application
sections.text: The range of application comprises non-financial corporates with consolidated annual revenue from EUR 25 million up to EUR 500 million (6,940 obligors, EAD EUR 16.8 billion, RWEA EUR 9.1 billion at 30 June 2026), booked in the Netherlands and the German and Belgian branches; groups are rated at the level of each obligor, with group support assessed as described in section 4.4. Corporates with revenue above EUR 500 million are rated by the large corporate model and their LGD and CCF are treated under the Foundation IRB approach; specialised lending and financial institutions are outside the range of application. All exposures of the corporate exposure class are under the IRB approach; the only permanent partial use is the corporate portfolio of the Luxembourg subsidiary (43 obligors, EAD EUR 0.2 billion), immaterial in size and risk profile under CRR Article 150(1), whose share of the corporate EAD (0.6%) is monitored quarterly against the 2% trigger of the roll-out plan. The roll-out plan for the corporate exposure class has been completed, and exposures are assigned to exposure classes by the documented assignment routine, applied in the same sequence since 2018.

sections.heading: Use in credit processes and internal parameters
sections.text: Ratings and PDs play an essential role in the Bank's credit processes: no credit is granted, renewed or restructured without a valid approved rating; the rating and exposure determine the approval authority (business-line authority up to grade C12 and EUR 10 million, Credit Risk Management above, Group Credit Committee for grades C17–C20 or above EUR 75 million); and the PD is used in pricing, limit setting, the credit risk appetite (EL and RWA density), internal capital allocation to Wholesale Banking and quarterly management reporting. The credit approval framework, including the approval authorities and the role of the rating, is laid down in the Credit Risk Policy CR-POL-001 approved by the Management Board. Credit decisions are never fully automated for corporates: the model output supports the creditworthiness assessment, and every decision is taken by authorised decision-makers under the four-eyes principle with independent approval by Credit Risk Management above the business-line authority, as required by CR-POL-001 §5.2 and §5.3. For IFRS 9 the PD is converted to a point-in-time, forward-looking lifetime PD without MoC in model MDL-08, and pricing uses the best-estimate PD without MoC; these differences are documented in the parameter mapping table PMT-PD-2026 and justified by the different purposes. All parameters used in the credit risk appetite metrics for mid-market corporates come from models registered in the inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system consists of clearly separated components: (a) a financial module, a logistic regression on seven financial ratios; (b) a qualitative module of eight questions; (c) the combination of both module scores into a rating score; (d) automatic notching for warning signals, outdated financial statements and group support; (e) the calibration of the score to a best-estimate PD and the assignment to the master scale; (f) the margin of conservatism; (g) the PD floor; and (h) the override process. The model follows a shadow-rating design in which the business risk profile (qualitative module) and the financial risk profile (financial module) are combined in the way rating agencies assess corporates; the qualitative weights were derived partly from external ratings (section 4.3), whereas the financial module and the calibration are based on the Bank's own default experience. The model is developed in-house; no vendor model or proprietary technology is used. The documentation of the rating process, the rating tool manual CorpRate v3 and the implementation specification allow a third party to understand, replicate and evaluate the assignment of obligors to grades.

sections.heading: Rating philosophy
sections.text: The model follows the Bank's hybrid rating philosophy: the financial ratios and the sector outlook and account conduct questions make grade assignment responsive to current obligor-specific and economic conditions, while the PD per grade is calibrated to the long-run average default rate. The expected dynamics are moderate grade migration over the cycle (in 2009 and 2020 the average grade deteriorated by 0.9 and 0.6 notches) and grade-level default rates that rise in downturns; the observed migration and yearly default rates per grade over 2008–2024 are consistent with this philosophy, as analysed in section 7.4. The rating scale reflects exclusively the risk of obligor default; facility characteristics such as collateral are not part of the rating.

sections.heading: Rating assignment process
sections.text: The account manager or credit analyst prepares the rating in CorpRate, including the financial statements spread in FinSpread and the qualitative answers with written justification; the rating is approved by a credit risk officer in Credit Risk Management who does not benefit from the credit decision. Ratings are reviewed at least annually, at least semi-annually for watchlist obligors, and whenever material new information becomes available (new financial statements, warning signals, restructuring); no new credit is granted to an obligor with a rating older than 12 months. The rating criteria, questions and answer guidelines are set out in the rating manual and applied identically in the Netherlands and the branches, so obligors with similar risk are assigned consistently to the same grade. All relevant and current information is considered in the rating: financial statements, management accounts, qualitative information and external information from credit registers and credit bureaux; where information is limited (for example outdated statements), the rating is more conservative. Where the credit officer has concerns about the accuracy of the information provided, reasonable enquiries and verification with the borrower and third parties are performed and documented before the rating is approved.

sections.heading: Dependencies and stress testing
sections.text: The model depends on the default register (target) and on FinSpread (inputs); its PDs are used by the corporate LGD model (MDL-07) for expected loss and by the IFRS 9 PD model (MDL-08). In the ICAAP and the EBA and internal stress tests, the rating grades are migrated with a satellite model linking grade migrations to GDP and sector variables, and the effect on own funds requirements of the severe but plausible recession scenario of the 2026 ICAAP was an RWEA increase of 14.2% for the range of application, reported to the Management Board with the ICAAP. The model complexity was assessed as Medium in the regular complexity assessment of MRM (October 2025); the model is not highly complex and not dynamic.

sections.heading: Reference data set and samples
sections.text: The model is recalibrated on the frozen RDS RDS-PDCORP-3.1 described in the approved RDS documentation EVD-06-RDS version 1.0 of 13 February 2026: 412,600 obligor-quarter observations with reference dates 2008–2024 and 1,386 default events. Data deficiencies DD-PD-01 and DD-PD-03 are carried into the limitations log and the MoC register. The calibration sample is the full RDS for all 68 reference dates, after the exclusions of RDS section 4.2; it is stored in the frozen RDS (table calib_sample) with 6,068 obligors per reference date on average. For the development of v3.0 in 2022 the samples were defined before estimation: development sample with reference dates 2008–2018 (70% random obligor split), out-of-sample the remaining 30% of obligors, and out-of-time sample reference dates 2019–2020; the out-of-time sample was not used for driver selection or estimation. For v3.1 the module coefficients were not re-estimated; their performance was re-tested on the post-development period 2021–2024 (99,800 obligor-quarters, 283 defaults), which serves as an additional out-of-time sample.

The calibration sample is the full RDS for all 68 reference dates, after the exclusions of RDS section 4.2; it is stored in the frozen RDS (table calib_sample) with 6,068 obligors per reference date on average.

For the development of v3.0 in 2022 the samples were defined before estimation: development sample with reference dates 2008–2018 (70% random obligor split), out-of-sample the remaining 30% of obligors, and out-of-time sample reference dates 2019–2020; the out-of-time sample was not used for driver selection or estimation.

For v3.1 the module coefficients were not re-estimated; their performance was re-tested on the post-development period 2021–2024 (99,800 obligor-quarters, 283 defaults), which serves as an additional out-of-time sample.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives, selection and selection bias
sections.text: For v3.0 four approaches were compared against regulatory compliance, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation criteria: (A) a two-module scorecard with logistic regression (selected), (B) a single logistic regression on financial and qualitative variables, (C) a pure shadow-rating model regressing agency-implied PDs on all drivers, and (D) a gradient boosting model. C was rejected because only 612 obligors (5% of the RDS) have an external rating and they are larger than the typical mid-market client; B performed comparably to A (out-of-time AUC 0.812 against 0.816) but mixed qualitative and financial information in a way credit officers found hard to challenge; D reached an out-of-time AUC of 0.846 but was rejected because of limited interpretability for credit decisions and the controls it would require. The selection of the less complex approach A is justified because its interpretability supports the use in credit decisions and challenge by credit officers; the gradient boosting model is retained as challenger (section 7.5). The model is applied to existing clients and prospects; declined prospects are few (4.2% of rated prospects in 2019–2024) and are rated with the same tool, so reject inference was not performed. The omission is justified by an analysis of the 214 declined prospects since 2019 that were subsequently financed by other banks: their default rate (2.8%) is in line with their assigned grades (average PD 2.6%), showing that selection bias has an immaterial effect on ranking.

sections.heading: Financial module
sections.text: The long list of 42 candidate ratios was compiled from literature, rating agency methodologies and the credit analysts of Wholesale Banking, and the expected sign of each ratio was stated before estimation. Variable selection combined univariate AUC and monotonicity tests, stability of the univariate AUC over the years, exclusion of one of each pair of ratios with a rank correlation above 0.6, and stepwise logistic regression with expert review of the candidate sets. The final seven ratios and their relative weights are: interest coverage (21%), net debt / EBITDA (19%), equity ratio (18%), return on assets (14%), current ratio (10%), log revenue (9%) and revenue growth (9%); all signs are as expected (higher coverage, equity, profitability, liquidity, size and growth lower the PD; higher leverage raises it) and all coefficients are significant at 1%. The ratios are available for every obligor at the point of use from the latest financial statement and were stable over the development period (yearly univariate AUC range below 0.08). The financial module has an AUC of 0.781 on the development sample.

sections.heading: Qualitative module and shadow-rating calibration of its weights
sections.text: The qualitative module contains eight questions with four to five answer categories: market position, management and governance, business model sustainability, customer and supplier concentration, sector outlook, financial flexibility, quality of financial reporting and account conduct. The weights were derived in two steps: a regression of the logit of the agency-implied one-year PD on the answers for the 612 externally rated obligors (R² 0.58), followed by a review by an expert panel of eight senior credit officers in May 2022, which increased the weight of account conduct from 8% to 12% and reduced market position from 18% to 14% because the internal default data showed stronger discriminatory power of account conduct; the panel and its elicitation are documented in EVD-06-EJ. The module has an AUC of 0.724 on internal defaults and its final weights were tested against the purely statistical weights, which give an AUC of 0.731; the impact of the expert adjustment on model performance is therefore small and was accepted in favour of interpretability.

sections.heading: Combination, warning signals and group support
sections.text: The module scores are combined in a logistic regression on internal defaults, giving weights of 64% to the financial and 36% to the qualitative module; the combined score has an AUC of 0.832 on the development sample. Warning signals lead to automatic downgrades of the grade after the score: financial covenant breach in the last 12 months (one notch), payment arrears above 30 days in the last three months (two notches), negative equity (two notches) and an adverse or disclaimed audit opinion (one notch), with a maximum cumulative downgrade of four notches; these rules reflect information not fully captured by the modules. Group support: where a stronger parent is assessed to provide strong or moderate support under the documented support assessment, the grade is improved by up to two or one notch respectively, never above the parent's grade. The notching rules were set by expert judgement (EJ-PD-03) and their impact was quantified: warning signal downgrades affect 7.4% of obligors and increase the AUC from 0.829 to 0.832; group support uplifts affect 4.1% of obligors and do not change the AUC.

sections.heading: Outdated financial statements
sections.text: Where the latest financial statement used in the rating is older than 18 months at the rating date, the tool applies a one-notch downgrade, and where it is older than 24 months a two-notch downgrade; ratings based on statements older than 36 months cannot be approved. The two-notch adjustment was chosen because obligors with statements older than 24 months had a default rate of 3.1% in 2016–2024, about two grades worse than their unadjusted average grade (C11, grade PD 0.98%) would imply; it is recorded as expert judgement EJ-PD-04 and supported by the sensitivity analysis in section 7.6. The remaining uncertainty is covered by MoC A-02.

sections.heading: Calibration target and long-run average default rate
sections.text: The PD is calibrated for one calibration segment, the whole range of application, to the long-run average of one-year default rates calculated quarterly with overlapping windows as the arithmetic average of the count-based default rates of the 68 reference dates 2008–2024; exposure weighting is not used. The observed average default rate is 1.55%; the default rates of 2020 and 2021 were strongly reduced by government support (GDP −3.9% in 2020 but default rate 1.6%), so, to reflect the likely range of variability, the one-year default rates of the eight reference dates in 2020–2021 were replaced by the rates predicted by the regression of default rates on GDP growth estimated on 2008–2019 (2.4% and 1.5%), which raises the LRA to 1.66%. The adjustment is an upward adjustment and is documented as expert judgement EJ-PD-05. At calibration segment level the LRA of 1.66% before MoC was compared with a reference LRA for the period 2008–2018 (1.81%); the difference is justified by the 2014 reduction of the share of construction and real estate development obligors, whose higher default rates inflate the reference period: re-weighting the 2008–2018 default rates to the sector mix of 2020–2024 gives a mix-adjusted reference LRA of 1.69%, which is close to the LRA used. Where the LRA falls below the higher of the five-year and all-data averages, the Bank would justify it; this is not the case, since the five-year average (2020–2024, 1.15% observed) is lower than the LRA.

sections.heading: Calibration method
sections.text: The combined score is transformed into a best-estimate PD with a logistic calibration function whose slope is retained from development (slope test on 2021–2024 data: 0.97, not significantly different from 1, p = 0.41) and whose intercept is set so that the average best-estimate PD over the calibration sample, after notching and overrides, equals the LRA of 1.66%. The calibration is performed on final grades after overrides and before the MoC and the regulatory floor, and it is monotone, so it does not change the rank ordering of obligors within the segment. Continuous PDs are used only to assign obligors to the master scale; the PD applied for own funds is the grade PD, and no smoothing is used to compensate for lack of data or low discriminatory power. The estimates are based on the Bank's historical default experience and empirical evidence of all relevant data, and are derived from the long-run average, not from judgement alone.

sections.heading: Master scale mapping, floors and grade distribution
sections.text: Each obligor is assigned by its best-estimate PD to one of the 20 non-defaulted grades C01–C20 of the Bank's non-retail master scale (plus default grade D), which exceeds the seven non-defaulted grades required by CRR Article 170(1)(b); each grade maps to exactly one master scale grade and grade PDs increase monotonically. Final grade PDs after MoC are, for example, C05 0.14%, C08 0.38%, C10 0.72%, C12 1.35%, C14 2.62%, C16 5.20%, C18 11.5% and C20 31.0%. The PD applied to each exposure is at least 0.05% in accordance with CRR Article 160(1); the floor is applied after the MoC and is binding for grades C01 and C02 (1.9% of obligors, 3.2% of EAD). 88% of obligors are in grades C06–C14; the largest grade (C10) holds 13.8% of obligors, below the 30% limit of CRM-STD-100 §5.4, and the portfolio's concentration in the middle of the scale is covered by enough grades with narrow PD bands.

sections.heading: Calibration tests
sections.text: Calibration tests were performed per grade and for the segment with the one-sided Jeffreys test and the exact binomial test of the grade PD (best estimate) against the observed default rates of the full calibration sample, and for each LRA calculation date the average best-estimate PD was compared with the one-year default rate and with the LRA. Results: portfolio p-value 0.47; one grade (C13) with p < 5% and none with p < 1%, which is within the green thresholds; the qualitative analysis confirms at least 20 obligors in every grade, no excessive concentration and a unimodal obligor distribution. The calibration therefore provides accurate and consistent quantitative estimates at grade level.

sections.heading: MoC framework and identification of deficiencies
sections.text: The MoC follows CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 section 4.4: the final PD is the best estimate after appropriate adjustments plus a MoC for category A (data and methodological deficiencies), category B (relevant changes) and category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 in the recalibration, including those raised by the 2025 annual validation; for each, an appropriate adjustment was considered first (the COVID-19 adjustment of the LRA is such an adjustment), and the MoC is not used for deficiencies that can be corrected. Deficiencies considered and rejected: the RateWise-to-CorpRate migration in 2014 (no effect on the calibration data), the missing qualitative answers 2008–2013 (affects only the module re-test) and the WHOA procedure (already reflected in the data).

sections.heading: MoC category A
sections.text: A-01 (default flag reconstruction 2008–2015, DD-PD-01): the LRA was re-estimated under three treatments of the P1 period (as reconstructed; P1 default rates increased by the 2.5% relative understatement estimated on P3 data; P1 default rates increased by the 3.9% missed-default rate without deduction of false defaults); the adverse effect ranges from +0.02 to +0.04 percentage points on the LRA, and the MoC is set at 2.4% of the grade PDs (+0.04 percentage points on average). A-02 (outdated financial statements, DD-PD-03): the notching rule of section 4.5 was compared with alternatives (one notch, three notches, grade-specific notching); the adverse effect on the portfolio average PD is +0.02 percentage points, set as MoC of 1.2% of the grade PDs. sections.heading: MoC category C
sections.text: Category C MoC is the difference between the upper bound of a one-sided 90% confidence interval of the LRA default rate and the LRA, computed with the variance of yearly default rates adjusted for their first-order autocorrelation (0.52): the upper bound is 1.75%, giving +0.09 percentage points or 5.4% of the LRA. At grade level the category C MoC is based on the distribution of the grade-level default rate estimator and therefore increases for grades with fewer observations: from 4.8% of the PD in C10 to 11.9% in C20.

sections.heading: MoC aggregation, register and effect
sections.text: The total MoC per grade is the sum of categories A, B and C without diversification; at portfolio level A is 3.6%, B 4.8% and C 5.4% of the best estimate, 13.8% in total (+0.23 percentage points), giving a portfolio-average final PD of 1.89% before floors. The MoC is applied multiplicatively per grade to the calibrated best-estimate grade PD before the floor, which preserves rank ordering: PDs after MoC increase monotonically with grade. The MoC register MOC-REG-MDL06 lists every deficiency with category, affected component and grades, quantification method, MoC value and remediation status, and the MDD documents the complete list of deficiencies with their category and methods. The total MoC is below 20% of the best estimate, so no redevelopment assessment is required under CRM-STD-101 §7.2. The MoC increases RWEA by EUR 312 million (A 82, B 109, C 121), reported per category in the quarterly MoC report, and MoC levels are reviewed in the annual review of estimates; a component is reduced only after confirmed remediation, and MoC changes are classified as model changes.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: The AUC of the combined rating (after notching and overrides) is 0.832 (Gini 0.664) on the development sample, 0.824 out-of-sample, 0.816 on the 2019–2020 out-of-time sample and 0.809 (Gini 0.618) on the 2021–2024 re-test sample, with a 95% DeLong confidence interval of 0.785–0.833 for the latter. The relative decrease of the Gini coefficient against development is 6.9%, which is green under the 10% and 20% thresholds, and the Gini is well above the red threshold of 0.45 for corporate PD models. By country the AUC on 2021–2024 is 0.812 (Netherlands), 0.794 (Germany) and 0.801 (Belgium), and by size class between 0.79 and 0.82.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: Realised default rates were compared with the grade PDs for every year 2008–2024: the rank ordering of default rates by grade holds in every year, grade-level default rates rise in 2009, 2012–2013 and fall in 2017–2019 and 2021–2022, and in each year at most three grades show a default rate outside the 95% Jeffreys interval of the best-estimate PD. On the 2021–2024 sample the observed default rate (1.02%) is below the average best-estimate PD (1.49%), which reflects the benign period and the support measures, not an overestimation of the long-run average. All performance metrics are within their thresholds, so no limitation had to be logged under MRM-STD-020 §8.3.

sections.heading: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of grades
sections.text: Heterogeneity: the default rates of adjacent grades differ significantly (one-sided test at 5%) for 17 of the 19 adjacent pairs; the exceptions are C01/C02 and C02/C03, which have very few defaults and are kept because they are needed for the large obligors near the floor; there are no significant overlaps of default risk between grades. Homogeneity: within each grade, the default rates of subsets by country, sector group, size class and financial statement age were tested against the rest of the grade; no subset with at least 200 obligor-quarters differs significantly after Bonferroni correction, except obligors with statements older than 24 months in grades C09–C12, which are addressed by the notching rule. The rating system therefore differentiates risk meaningfully and groups obligors with similar default risk.

sections.heading: Stability and rating migration
sections.text: The PSI of the score between the development sample and the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 is 0.05; the twelve-month migration matrix for 2025 shows 71% of obligors within one notch and 6.4% migrating by more than two grades. The upper and lower matrix weighted bandwidths are 0.43 and 0.39 (v3.0 initial validation: 0.40 and 0.37), and the pairwise z-tests of off-diagonal transition frequencies show no significant non-monotonicity. The Herfindahl index of the grade distribution is 0.071, with no significant change of its coefficient of variation against the initial validation. Design stability was tested by re-estimating the financial module on reference dates 2012–2020 and 2016–2024: all coefficients keep their sign and differ by less than 25% from the development coefficients.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, the rating is compared with the gradient boosting challenger of section 4.1: on 2021–2024 the challenger reaches an AUC of 0.838 against 0.809, driven mainly by non-linear effects of leverage and revenue growth; the difference is explained and the model is retained because of interpretability for credit decisions, the small effect on the capital requirement (RWEA −1.4% with challenger PDs) and the controls the challenger would require. External benchmark: for the 612 obligors with an agency rating the Spearman rank correlation between internal grade and agency rating is 0.71; internal grades were mapped to the S&P scale by comparing the rating criteria, the grades of common obligors and the default definitions (the agency definition excludes UTP defaults without missed payment), with C06–C07 corresponding to BBB-, C10 to BB and C14 to B+. The mapping is used only for benchmarking and not for calibration, so it cannot bias the PD estimates.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key choices: LRA window (2008–2018 only 1.81%; without the COVID-19 adjustment 1.55%), notching for outdated statements (one notch: portfolio PD −0.4%; three notches: +0.3%), qualitative weights (statistical instead of expert weights: AUC +0.001, RWEA −0.6%), warning-signal notching removed (RWEA −1.9%) and group support removed (RWEA +2.3%). The results are documented with their effect on the model output and were used to support the MoC quantification in chapter 6. The sensitivity analysis also shows the circumstances in which the model is less reliable (section 8.3).

sections.heading: Climate-related and environmental risks
sections.text: Climate-related and environmental risks were assessed for materiality in the 2025 annual review using the Bank's sector heatmap: 18% of the EAD is in sectors with high transition risk (transport, chemicals, agriculture), and the sector outlook question of the qualitative module was extended in v3.0 with guidance to consider transition risk; no additional climate driver was included because the default data show no significant effect after controlling for the existing drivers (p = 0.37). The assessment will be repeated at each annual review.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: Material assumptions are: (1) the relationship between financial ratios and default is stable over time; (2) the qualitative answers are applied consistently by credit analysts; (3) the 2020–2021 default rates understate the risk of those economic conditions because of support measures; (4) the current sector mix will remain; and (5) the notching rules adequately compensate for information not in the modules. Assumption 1 is supported by the stability tests in section 7.4, assumption 2 by the consistency reviews of rating quality by Credit Risk Management, assumption 3 by the GDP regression, and assumptions 4 and 5 by the sensitivity analyses and the MoC.

sections.heading: Circumstances in which the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The model is not suitable for start-ups without two years of financial statements, holding companies without operations, project and object finance, public sector entities and corporates in financial restructuring; such obligors are rated with the specialised tools or the expert module and the rating manual prohibits the use of PD-CORP-MM for them. The model may underestimate risk where financial statements are outdated or in very rapid sector shocks not yet visible in the statements; the warning signals and overrides mitigate this.

sections.heading: Implementation specification, handover and production controls
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-PDCORP-3.1 (approved by the Model Owner on 9 March 2026) is consistent with this MDD and defines inputs, source fields and lineage, ratio definitions, caps, missing value rules, coefficients, notching rules, calibration function, master scale mapping, MoC factors, PD floor, override rules and rounding. The handover package contained the specification, the parameter file params_v3.1.0.json, 2,400 test cases with expected outputs from the development code, including boundary, missing and invalid inputs and every grade, and reference outputs for the portfolio at 31 December 2025. Implementation testing, the reconciliation with the development outputs and the parallel run are performed by the PD engine team and Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling and documented in the implementation and testing report EVD-06-IMPL. All parameters of CorpRate and of the PD engine (coefficients, caps, calibration function, master scale, MoC factors, notching rules) are version-controlled parameter tables with restricted access, changed only through the model change and approval process; model developers have no write access to production. Each rating stores the model and parameter version used, and the monthly PD engine run logs reference date, input data version, code version and parameter version.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan – KPIs, frequency and responsibilities
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-PDCORP-3.1 is approved by the Model Owner and reviewed by Model Validation; it defines the KPIs and their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference periods, segments (country and size class), responsible persons and escalation. KPIs are PSI of score, grades and drivers, AUC/Gini on the latest one-year window, Jeffreys and binomial tests per grade and portfolio, migration and concentration statistics, override rates by direction, reason, magnitude and approving unit, overlays, production data quality and model coverage (share of obligors with a valid rating and share of outdated ratings). Monitoring is quarterly for the Tier 1 model, with calibration KPIs on rolling one-year windows; reports are finalised within 60 days after quarter-end and show value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four quarters, and the monitoring code is version-controlled (tag mon-v3.1.0) so results are reproducible. The plan is updated with every model change and reviewed at least annually; it was last updated for v3.1 in March 2026.

sections.heading: Monitoring thresholds and escalation
sections.text: Thresholds: PSI green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25; relative Gini decrease above 10% amber and above 20% red, and a Gini below 0.40 red regardless of change; calibration amber if the portfolio p-value is below 5% or more than 20% of grades are below 5%, red if the portfolio p-value is below 1% or more than 30% of grades are below 1%; override rate above 10% amber and above 20% red. Amber results are analysed by the Model Owner; a red result or two consecutive ambers on the same KPI are notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 days proposing no action, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use; red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the MRC. A red outcome leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the MRC within three months, and results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and an additional MoC. Monitoring results are sent to Credit Risk Management, which uses them in the credit risk reporting and in the review of the credit approval framework.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates
sections.text: The framework for the regular review of estimates defines the minimum scope, frequency, metrics, thresholds and significance levels, and the actions for adverse results: at least annually and whenever new information comes to light, the review analyses the representativeness of the RDS against the application portfolio, model performance and its stability on the whole application portfolio per period against development, and predictive power, including whether recent data change the LRA materially, with back-testing per grade. Predictive power is analysed at grade level with the Jeffreys and binomial tests, the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and charts of default rates against PDs per grade. The annual model review also covers portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the Model Owner and is provided to MRM and Model Validation. The 2025 review (report of 30 October 2025) concluded that the model remains fit for purpose and that the annual recalibration documented here was required, including the extension of the data window with 2024; the MoC for the reconstructed default flag was reassessed with the longer P3 period. Where realised default rates exceed the grade PDs beyond the red threshold in two consecutive annual reviews, taking the cycle into account, the PDs are revised upward; methods and data are kept consistent over time and any change is documented in the review report.

sections.heading: Validation cycle
sections.text: As a Tier 1 IRB model the rating system is validated annually by Model Validation – Credit Risk, with a full-scope validation at least every three years (last full validation: initial validation of v3.0 in 2023; next in 2026). Model Validation is independent of Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling and of Wholesale Banking, reports through the Head of Model Risk Management to the CRO, and its staff did not contribute to the model development. For v3.1, a non-material change to a Tier 1 model, Model Validation decided on 17 November 2025, within ten business days of the change notification, to perform a targeted pre-implementation review (MV-2026-CR-004), which concluded on 2 March 2026 without high or medium findings. The statistical validation process, including out-of-sample and out-of-time tests, is set out in chapter 7 and in the monitoring plan.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: The expert judgement log EJ-LOG-MDL06, stored with the model documentation, records for each judgement its type, life cycle stage, affected component, rationale, evidence, alternatives considered and rejected, quantified impact, proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry conditions. Entries: EJ-PD-01 selection of the final financial ratios (design; medium); EJ-PD-02 expert adjustment of the qualitative weights (design; RWEA −0.6%; medium); EJ-PD-03 warning signal and group support notching (design; RWEA +1.9% and −2.3%; medium); EJ-PD-04 notching for outdated statements (design; +0.4% portfolio PD; low); EJ-PD-05 COVID-19 adjustment of the LRA (calibration; LRA +0.11 percentage points, RWEA +3.1%; medium); EJ-PD-06 imputation rules; EJ-PD-07 scope corrections of wrongly assigned obligors (data; LRA +0.02 pp; low). Each rationale refers to specific analyses (regression output, default rates by statement age, panel minutes), so a third party can replicate the effect; unsupported references to experience are not used. All judgements were reviewed in the 2025 annual review; EJ-PD-05 expires when the LRA window no longer contains 2020–2021 or when a counterfactual is no longer needed.

sections.heading: Override policy, monitoring and performance
sections.text: Overrides of the model grade are permitted only on the basis of relevant information not captured by the model, using the closed list of nine reason codes of the rating manual (for example imminent loss of a key contract, pending litigation, unaudited recent figures showing material change, parental support not captured by the notching rule). Each override is documented in CorpRate with reason code, written rationale, supporting evidence, proposer and approver, and is approved by Credit Risk Management independently of the proposer; the default grade D and the fraud warning signal cannot be overridden. The maximum override is three notches; upward overrides are more restricted than downward overrides: upward overrides of more than two notches require approval by the Group Credit Committee, and upward overrides may not exceed 5% of ratings per quarter, while downward overrides may be approved by any credit risk officer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly by country, reason and approving unit; rates above 10% are analysed by the Model Owner and reported to MRM. The performance of overrides is analysed annually: in 2016–2024 the default rate of downward-overridden obligors was 2.9% against 1.4% for their pre-override grades and 3.0% for their final grades, and that of upward-overridden obligors 0.9% against 1.2% pre-override; the overrides therefore improve discriminatory power (AUC 0.829 before and 0.832 after overrides). Systematic overrides would be treated as an indication of model deficiency; the most frequent reason (unaudited recent figures, 31% of overrides) is addressed by the monitoring of statement age.

sections.heading: Change classification and regulatory status
sections.text: The recalibration updates the LRA with the latest data, re-quantifies the MoC with the existing methodology and leaves methodology, drivers, rating philosophy, default definition and range of application unchanged; it is therefore not internally material, and under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 it is a non-material change notified ex post (Class C). The impact was computed on 31 December 2025 on the same exposures before and after the change: RWEA of the range of application −0.9% and Bank-wide credit RWEA −0.26%, below the 5% and 1.5% thresholds, and 8.1% of obligors change grade, below the 10% threshold of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e). MRM confirmed the classification on 24 November 2025; the change, planned for implementation on 1 April 2026, will be included in the ex post notification to the ECB for the second quarter of 2026, with description, rationale, implementation date, scope, internal approval and impact. The two obligations of the ECB permission of 2024 (monitoring of the override rate and reassessment of the COVID-19 treatment in the LRA) are recorded in the inventory with owner and deadline and tracked as MRC conditions; this recalibration addresses the second obligation.

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the RDS RDS-PDCORP-3.1 for the recalibration of PD-CORP-MM v3.1 (MDL-06), performed from 12 to 29 January 2026 by Wholesale Credit Risk Modelling and the Wholesale Data Quality team before the RDS was frozen; it also serves as the DQ assessment of the data used for the annual validation. It applies MRM-STD-022 v2.2, which forms the Bank's data quality management framework for all data used in IRB processes, and DATA-POL-001, which applies chapter 3.2 of the ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting to all model inputs and is approved by the Management Board. The dimensions assessed are completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness and appropriateness.

sections.heading: Critical data elements, DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: Sixteen critical data elements are defined: the balance sheet and income statement items behind the seven ratios, the statement date, the eight qualitative answers (as one CDE group), the grade before and after override, the override reason, the obligor scope attributes (revenue, NACE code, country), the default flag and the default date; each has at least one DQ rule per applicable dimension, and the reason is recorded where a dimension does not apply. The 71 rules are listed in Annex 1 and in RDS Annex A; 52 recurring rules run monthly in the Group DQ monitoring tool DQ Monitor on production data. Thresholds are the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3 (completeness amber below 98%, red below 95%; accuracy amber above 0.5%, red above 1% difference; consistency amber below 99%, red below 98%), with stricter thresholds for the default flag and default date (completeness and accuracy red below 99.5%); no less strict threshold is applied. Checks run from data entry (validation rules in FinSpread and CorpRate) through the reconciliations between LoanIQ, the risk data warehouse and the finance ledger to the reports, and controls over these risk data are as robust as those over accounting data.

sections.heading: Completeness
sections.text: Record level: all obligors in scope in LoanIQ at each reference date are present in the RDS (difference 0 after scope corrections), and all 1,427 default events of in-scope obligors in the default register are present before the exclusion of technical past due events. Attribute level: financial statement items are 98.2–100% complete; qualitative answers are 89% complete for 2008–2013 (amber; RateWise stored only module scores) and 99.9% from 2014; the default flag and date are 100% complete. The gap in qualitative answers affects only the re-test of the qualitative weights and not the calibration; its effect on the reliability of the results is assessed in RDS section 6.2 (DD-PD-02).

sections.heading: Accuracy and reconciliation
sections.text: Accuracy was measured by reconciling exposures and drawn amounts with LoanIQ and the finance ledger (maximum difference 0.04%), by reconciling all default events with the default register maintained under CR-STD-110, and by comparing financial statement data with independent sources. As required for a Tier 1 model, a sample of 250 obligor-years was verified against the audited financial statements in the credit files: 243 agreed in all ratio inputs, 7 showed spreading differences (reclassification of shareholder loans), of which none changed the grade by more than one notch; the spreading guideline was clarified in October 2025. Critical data elements are reconciled with source systems and accounting data at least annually, unexplained differences are recorded as DQ issues, and the RDS is consistent with the data used for COREP credit risk reporting.

sections.heading: Consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness
sections.text: Consistency: logical rules (total assets equal liabilities plus equity; EBITDA not below operating profit minus depreciation; revenue consistent with the size class) pass for 99.6% of statements, and default rates and driver distributions are consistent over time, including across the three default-definition regimes. Consistency between the RDS and the production input data: for the 2025 reference dates the ratios computed by the RDS build code and by CorpRate agree for 99.8% of obligors; the differences concern restated statements. sections.heading: Elicitation method
sections.text: A two-round Delphi procedure was used: in round one each expert ranked and weighted the eight qualitative questions independently and justified the weights in writing, having received the statistical weights from the shadow-rating regression and the internal default analysis; in round two the anonymised results were discussed and each expert revised the weights individually. The individual contributions of both rounds are recorded in Annex 1, and the aggregation used the median of the round-two weights, rescaled to 100%.

sections.heading: Outcome on the qualitative weights (EJ-PD-02)
sections.text: The panel increased the weight of account conduct from 8% (statistical) to 12% and reduced market position from 18% to 14%, on the evidence that account conduct had a univariate AUC of 0.68 on internal defaults against 0.61 for market position, and that market position was often assessed optimistically for family-owned companies. Alternatives considered and rejected: the pure statistical weights (rejected because the regression on 612 large obligors under-represents account conduct for smaller clients) and equal weights (lower AUC 0.709). The quantified impact is an AUC of the qualitative module of 0.724 instead of 0.731 and an RWEA change of −0.6%, so the judgement is of medium materiality.

sections.text: The panel confirmed the warning signals and their notches on the basis of default rates of obligors with each signal in 2012–2021 (for example covenant breach: default rate 4.8% against 1.6% for the same grades without breach) and set the maximum cumulative downgrade at four notches. For outdated financial statements the panel set a one-notch downgrade above 18 months and two notches above 24 months, based on the default rate of 3.1% for obligors with statements older than 24 months; the 2025 panel reviewed the rule with 2016–2024 data and kept it unchanged. Each rule's impact was quantified by sensitivity analysis under reasonable alternatives (one to three notches) and is reported in MDD section 7.6.

documents.title: Implementation and testing report PD-CORP-MM v3.1

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: This report documents the implementation of PD-CORP-MM v3.1 in the rating tool CorpRate (score, notching, grade, override workflow) and in the PD engine of RiskCalc (grade PD, MoC, floor), and the tests performed before go-live on 1 April 2026 under the Bank's documented, organisation-wide IRB system testing process. Because v3.1 changes only parameters (calibration intercept, grade PDs, MoC factors), the scope was a parameter release with full regression testing.

sections.heading: Implementation specification and lineage
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-PDCORP-3.1, approved by the Model Owner on 9 March 2026, defines the production source field and lineage of every input and identifies no difference between development and production data sources; the lineage of the development and production input data was compared and the ratio calculations were found identical. sections.text: Production input data are checked with the DQ rules of the RDS; each rating stores the model and parameter version, each PD engine run logs reference date, input version, code and parameter version, and manual reruns require an approved ticket and are logged. sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The realised default rate of the window is 1.22% against an average best-estimate PD of 1.47% for the cohort; the one-sided Jeffreys test at portfolio level, reporting the Beta(D+1/2, N−D+1/2) distribution function at the PD as p-value, gives p = 0.97 (green), and per grade one grade (C15, 11 defaults among 212 obligors, PD 3.4%) has p = 0.03 and none p < 1% (green). The binomial test gives the same result, and the default rates per grade increase monotonically except for an insignificant inversion between C04 and C05. The deviation in C15 was analysed: 6 of the 11 defaults are in the construction sector after the 2025 nitrogen permit rulings, and it is monitored in the next quarters.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 5.1 justifies the LRA of 1.66% against the 2008–2018 reference LRA (1.81%) with a sector-mix adjustment to 1.69%. Model Validation recomputed the reference LRA keeping obligors that migrated to other models or were repaid during the year in the denominator and numerator, and re-weighted only within size classes as well as sectors: the mix-adjusted reference LRA is 1.78%, so the sector-mix argument explains only about 0.03 of the 0.15 percentage-point gap and the lower LRA is not sufficiently justified.

mitigation.text: Recompute the reference LRA on the same default rate definition as the calibration (EBA/GL/2017/16 para 76), document the mix adjustment per size class and sector, and either justify the remaining gap with evidence or raise the LRA or the category B MoC accordingly.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 4.5 documents a two-notch downgrade for financial statements older than 24 months, based on a 3.1% default rate. Model Validation's analysis of the 2021–2025 windows shows a default rate of 4.6% for these obligors against an average PD after notching of 2.1%, and the Jeffreys test rejects the adjusted PD at the 1% level; the adjustment is therefore not adequately conservative and MoC A-02 does not cover the gap.

mitigation.text: Recalibrate the notching for outdated financial statements (for example three notches above 24 months or a PD multiplier derived from observed default rates), requantify MoC A-02 and reinforce the collection of statements through Wholesale Credit Operations.

deficiencies.rationale: The revenue growth PSI has been amber for three consecutive quarters; the trigger was notified on 28 May 2026, but the root cause analysis and action plan due within 60 days (27 July 2026) had not been submitted by the Q2 2026 report of 25 August 2026.

mitigation.text: Submit the root cause analysis and action plan for the revenue growth PSI to MRM and Model Validation (proposal: replace nominal by real revenue growth at the next model change) and record the delay in the monitoring log.

deficiencies.rationale: The MDD and RDS documentation use quarterly overlapping one-year windows as prescribed by CRM-STD-100 §8.2, but do not document an analysis of the bias from overlapping windows, calculation dates, short-term contracts and seasonality supporting this choice against non-overlapping windows.

mitigation.text: Add to MDD section 5.1 an analysis comparing the LRA from overlapping and non-overlapping (annual, different calculation dates) windows, including seasonality of defaults and short-term facilities, and document the conclusion.

deficiencies.rationale: Override performance is reported only as aggregate default rates of downward and upward overrides against their pre-override grades; realised default rates by original and final grade are not shown, so it cannot be assessed per grade whether overrides improve the assignment.

mitigation.text: Extend the annual override performance analysis and the monitoring report with a matrix of realised default rates by original and final grade, per direction and reason code.
